Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States

Current Data

This page provides current data and interactive features to supplement the Sabin Center’s report on Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States: September 2026 Edition. Click on the map below to read about: (a) state and local restrictions that impede the siting and deployment of large-scale wind, solar, and battery storage projects, as well as related transmission projects; and (b) individual examples of contested projects that have faced significant opposition, including lawsuits and other actions, during the siting process. Note that some contested projects span multiple counties but each project is only counted once in calculating state totals.

You can download the Restriction data and the Contested Project data.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   This database is updated on a monthly basis. The last update was September 8, 2026.

 

*This map reflects only local restrictions currently in effect. Information on expired restrictions may be accessed via the state drop down menu below.

Alabama

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. State legislation expressly grants 4 counties – Baldwin, Cherokee, Dekalb, and Etowah – zoning authority over wind projects. The legislation specifies that a county permit is required for any wind project in Cherokee, Dekalb, and Etowah counties. In Baldwin County, the county commissioner can choose whether or not to require county permits for wind energy projects. State legislation does not expressly address solar energy project siting but, in practice, siting decisions are made at the local level.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

Ala. Admin. Code §§ 45-2-262 (Baldwin), 45-10-260.02 (Cherokee), 45-25-260.02 (Dekalb), 45-28-260.02 (Etowah).

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Local Restrictions

Restrictions with Status In effect
  • Baldwin County

    Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind)
    The Baldwin County Zoning Ordinance, as amended in May of 2025, provides that wind energy systems with a capacity of 50 kW or greater are prohibited in all zoning districts. Any small wind energy system located near a scenic byway or corridor must not cause an adverse visual impact.

    Baldwin County, Ala., Zoning Ordinance §§ 13.13.4, 13.13.6(j) (Oct. 18, 2022), https://baldwincountyal.gov/docs/default-source/plannin-zoning/ordinances-and-regulations/zoning-ordinance-(updated-5-20-2025).pdf?sfvrsn=c1b4d700_3

  • Cherokee County

    Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 402, which established certain restrictions on wind power in Cherokee County, including: (1) a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the nearest property line; and (2) a setback of at least 2,500 feet from the nearest property line.

    Cherokee County, Ala., Act No. 2014-190, S.B. 402 §§ 6(i)-(j) (Mar. 18, 2014), https://legiscan.com/AL/text/SB402/id/991772/Alabama-2014-SB402-Enrolled.pdf

  • DeKalb County

    Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    In DeKalb County, wind turbines must be set back 2,500 feet from property lines and noise must not exceed 40 decibels. In addition, any wind energy system or turbine “that does not operate continuously for 365 consecutive days may be deemed abandoned and shall be removed by the operator of the system.”

    DeKalb County, Ala., Ala. Code § 45-25-260.05 (Sept. 1, 2015), https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-45/chapter-25/article-26/part-1/section-45-25-260-05/

  • Etowah County

    Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 403, which established certain restrictions on wind power in Etowah County, including: (1) a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the nearest property line; and (2) a setback of at least 2,500 feet from the nearest property line.

    Etowah County, Act No. 2014-191, S.B. 403 §§ 6(i)-(j) (Mar. 19, 2014), https://legiscan.com/AL/text/SB403/id/992930/Alabama-2014-SB403-Enrolled.pdf

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Noccalula Wind Energy Center (Etowah County)

    In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy, a Texas-based developer, abandoned plans to construct a $160 million wind project comprising 35 to 40 turbines after local residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous restrictions on wind energy in Etowah County.

    William Thorton, Wind Energy Company Pulling out of Cherokee, Etowah County Projects, Opposition Says, Anniston-Gadsden Real-Time News, Aug. 19, 2014, https://www.al.com/news/anniston-gadsden/2014/08/pioneer_green_energy_pulling_o.html.

  • Shinbone Ridge Wind (Cherokee County)

    In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans to construct a $40 million wind project comprising 7 to 8 wind turbines in Cherokee County after local residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous restrictions on wind energy in Cherokee County.

    William Thornton, Alabama Regs Too Strict for Turbines, Says Lawyer for Wind Energy Developer, Anniston-Gadsden Real-Time News, Aug. 20, 2014, https://www.al.com/news/anniston-gadsden/2014/08/alabama_regs_too_strict_for_tu.html; Complaint for Permanent Injunction, Shaver et al. v.   • Turkey Heaven Mountain Wind (Cleburne County)

    In October 2015, Native Energy Solutions, an Oklahoma-based developer, announced that it was no longer planning to build a wind project in Cleburne County. The project faced opposition from local residents who, in June 2014, filed a lawsuit seeking a permanent injunction that would bar the developer from constructing wind turbines in the County, citing concerns about “wind turbine syndrome” among other things. The developer filed a motion to dismiss, but the motion was denied.

    Laura Camper, Wind Turbine Company Has No Plans for Alabama After Lawsuit from Cleburne County Homeowners, The Anniston Star, Oct. 20, 2015, https://www.annistonstar.com/news/wind-turbine-company-has-no-plans-for-alabama-after-lawsuit-from-cleburne-county-homeowners/article_30289b7e-775c-11e5-a572-f775a9d8f777.html; Doggett v. Projects with Status Pending
  • Origis Energy Solar Farm (Covington County)

    Local residents expressed strong opposition to a proposed solar farm at an August 21, 2023 meeting reviewing the possible construction of a 160-MW, 1,000-acre solar panel array. The residents opposed the farm for several reasons, including that the farm would be powering communities “over an hour away” and not their own; that the solar farm might encroach on family properties that have existed for generations; and that potential road runoff might impact their well water supplies. Residents also expressed frustration that surveyors had entered their property without their permission. An online petition created by the group “Concerned Citizens of Covington County Alabama” urged Origis Energy to relocate the project to a more remote or industrial area of Covington County. As of December 31, 2023, the petition had 80 signatures.

    Robert Blankenship, Oakey Ridge residents adamantly oppose solar farm, Andalusia Star News, Aug. 22, 2023, https://www.andalusiastarnews.com/2023/08/22/oakey-ridge-residents-adamantly-oppose-solar-farm/; Save Covington County from Toxic Solar Farms, Care2 Petitions, https://www.thepetitionsite.com/413/135/680/save-covington-county-from-toxic-solar-farms/ (last visited Jan. 31, 2024)

  • Stockton I and Stockton II Solar (Baldwin County)

    In October 2025, Alabama Power submitted its proposal for two solar projects, the 80-MW Stockton I and the 180-MW Stockton II, to be located on approximately 2,000 acres of land in Stockton. The projects were designed to power a Meta-affiliated data center under construction in Montgomery. Local residents have voiced concerns about the projects, including the impacts on the community’s rural character and wetlands as well as its proximity to the Mobile-Tensaw Delta and the potential environmental risks posed by hurricanes and flooding. The opponents created a Facebook page titled “Stop Solar in Stockton,” where residents have raised concerns about land use, environmental impacts, and the lack of public notice. In December 2025, the Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously approved the projects. Construction is expected to begin in 2026, with commercial operation by the end of 2028.

    Brad Gunther, NBC 15 Reality Check: Records raise questions on timing of Stockton solar project approval, NBC15, Feb. 6, 2026, https://mynbc15.com/news/reality-check/nbc-15-reality-check-records-raise-questions-on-timing-of-stockton-solar-project-approval.

Alaska

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects less than 65 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over larger projects (65 MW or larger). These larger projects require a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Regulatory Commission of Alaska.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

 

Alaska Stat. §§ 29.40.040; 42.05.221; 42.05.711(r)(1)(B); 42.05.711(s)(1).

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Arizona

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind energy projects of any size and solar energy projects less than 100 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over larger solar energy projects (100 MW or more). A certificate of environmental compatibility (CEC) from the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee is required for these larger solar projects.

One or more public hearings are required as part of the CEC application process and the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee is required to grant or deny a CEC within 180 days of an application being filed.

 

Ariz. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 40-360.06, 40-360, 40- 360.05, 40-360, 360.03.

State-Level Restrictions

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Black Mesa Pumped Storage Project (Apache and Navajo Counties)

    The developer Nature and People First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on approximately 400 acres of land. In July 2023, three organizations—Tó Nizhóní Ání, Diné Citizens Against Ruining our Environment, and Center for Biological Diversity—submitted a letter to FERC attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had expressed concerns that the project could damage underground water supplies and sacred lands and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project, stating that “[t]he Commission will not issue preliminary permits for projects proposing to use Tribal lands if the Tribes on whose land the project is to be located opposes the permit.”

    Renee Romo, Hydropower project at Black Mesa on Navajo Nation draws opponents, KJZZ, Dec. 27, 2023, https://kjzz.org/content/1866630/hydropower-project-black-mesa-navajo-nation-draws-opponents; Kianna Joe, ‘Tó Iiná’, Bodaway-Gap Chapter Passes Resolution Opposing Pumped Storage Project Targeting Dziłyíjiin, Navajo Times, May 25, 2023, https://navajotimes.com/reznews/to-iina-bodaway-gap-chapter-passes-resolution-opposing-pumped-storage-project-targeting-dzilyijiin/; 18 Navajo Nation Chapter and Agency Resolutions Opposing Project, FERC Case Nos. 15233-000, 15234-000, and 15235-000 (July 14, 2023), https://www.biologicaldiversity.org/programs/public_lands/rivers/pdfs/14-July-23-TNA-DINECARE-Center-FERC-FILING.pdf; Alex Hager, Federal energy regulators deny permits for a controversial project on the Navajo Nation, KUNC, Feb. 16, 2024, https://www.kunc.org/news/2024-02-16/federal-energy-regulators-deny-permits-for-a-controversial-project-on-the-navajo-nation; In re Nature and People First Arizona PHS, LLC, Order Denying Applications for Preliminary Permit, 186 FERC ¶ 61,117 (Feb. 15, 2024), https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/public_lands/rivers/pdfs/20240215-Order-Denying-Preliminary-Permit-Black-Mesa.pdf.

    On September 11, 2024, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission voted to deny a special use permit to construct a 75-MW solar farm on 597 acres of land. In voting to deny the project, the commission chairwoman stated, “We’ve got too many of these in the county now.”

    Shar Porier, County P&Z Denies Special Use Permit for Solar Farm, Herald Review, Sept. 13, 2024, https://www.myheraldreview.com/county-p-z-denies-special-use-permit-for-solar-farm/article_0c16d914-71fb-11ef-8e52-eb0ef4ea0281.html.

  • Silver King Energy Center (Pinal County)

    In 2025, Arevia Power proposed the Silver King Energy Center, a hybrid facility with 800 MW of solar energy generation and 400 MW of thermal energy generation, to be located on approximately 8,122 acres of public lands north of Florence and east of San Tan Valley. On January 15, 2026, the County Planning and Zoning Commission, in a 4-3 vote, recommended denial of three rezoning applications that would have allowed the project to move forward. On February 18, 2026, the County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to reject the project rezoning applications. Opponents of the project expressed concerns about the visual impacts of solar panels on the desert landscape, the potential safety implications of locating a large utility-scale facility adjacent to the towns, and the impacts on the future of freeway construction. Supporters of the project noted the project benefits including significant job opportunities during construction, long-term operational jobs, and the substantial tax revenue for Pinal County and for public education, primarily lease payment revenue for the Arizona State University.

    Kevin Reagan, Elected officials reject solar farm on 8,000 acres near San Tan Valley, 12 NEWS, Feb. 19, 2026, https://www.12news.com/article/news/local/arizona/elected-officials-reject-solar-farm-on-8000-acres-san-tan-valley-florence-arizona-pinal-county/75-df1d8656-c5b1-45d9-9576-9955402bd85b; Broad coalition backs Silver King Energy Center ahead of Pinal County zoning vote, CHAMBER BUSINESS NEWS, Feb. 8, 2026, broad-coalition-backs-silver-king-energy-center-ahead-of-pinal-county-zoning-vote; Justin Matthews,County’s Largest Energy Project Stumbles At Planning Commission, PINAL POST, Jan. 16, 2026, https://pinalpost.com/countys-largest-energy-project-stumbles-at-planning-commission/; Silver King Energy Center, https://www.silverkingenergycenter.com/ (last visited May 22, 2026).

Projects with Status Pending
  • Lava Run Solar (Apache County)

    In 2025, Repsol proposed the 450 MW Lava Solar Project to be located on approximately 3,700 acres of public lands in Apache County. The developer has also proposed to construct a 27-mile transmission line that would serve the Lava Run Wind and the Lava Run Solar projects.

    The project has faced strong opposition from a group called “Stop Lava Run” that was formed with the sole purpose of opposing the Lava Run Solar and Lava Run Wind projects. The group maintains a website encouraging local residents to file public comments in opposition to the project and attend public hearings to raise concerns, including the project’s potential impacts on wildlife and ecosystems, water pollution as well as impacts on hunting, recreation, and tourism.

    In September 2025, the developer submitted an application for a Certificate of Environmental Compatibility (CEC) to the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee (LSC). In October 2025, the LSC, in an 8-2 vote, recommended approval of the CEC. In December 2025, the Arizona Corporate Commission unanimously voted to send the application back to the LSC to more fully address the concerns raised by local residents in opposition to the project.

  • SunZia Transmission Line (Cochise County)

    The SunZia transmission line is designed to transmit more than 3,600 MW of electricity generated at wind farms in New Mexico. Its routing in the San Pedro Valley prompted controversy, with the Tohono O’odham, Hopi, Zuni, and San Carlos Apache tribes claiming that the Bureau of Land Management ignored over 15 years of attempts by the tribes to recognize the valley as a culturally significant area. In January 2024, the Tohono O’odham Nation, San Carlos Apache Tribe, Center for Biological Diversity, and Archeology Southwest filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, claiming that the review of the project violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The lawsuit was dismissed in June 2024 and subsequently appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. In May 2025, the Court of Appeals reversed the district court’s dismissal and remanded the case for further proceedings.  In April 2026, the developer, Pattern Energy, began testing the project as it nears completion. The lawsuit challenging the project remains pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona.

Arkansas

State Siting Framework

Local governments in Arkansas have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects less than 50 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of larger wind and solar projects (50 MW or more in size). A certificate of environmental compatibility and public need (CECPN) must be obtained from the Arkansas Public Service Commission for these larger projects. The Commission must hold a public hearing on an application for a CECPN at least 40, and not more than 180, days after receipt of the application. The Commission must issue a decision within 60 days after the public hearing.

 

A.C.A. §§ 14-17-205, 23-18-503(6), 23-18-504, 23-18-510, 23-18-519.

State-Level Restrictions

Restrictions with Status In effect
  • Arkansas Wind Energy Development Act

    Rule 6a and 6b: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    In April 2025, the Arkansas legislature enacted the Wind Energy Development Act (SB437) which was signed into law on April 22, 2025. The law became effective on August 3, 2025, though its implementing rules (adopted on January 14, 2026) are still pending Legislative Council approval. The law  created Arkansas’ first statewide permitting regime for wind energy facilities of at least 5 megawatts (MW) and exceeding 200 feet in height. The law requires a minimum setback from non-participating property lines of 3.5 times the total height of the wind turbines or 2,500 feet, whichever is greater and a 1-mile setback from a school, hospital, nursing home or church. The law provides that the noise level from wind turbines at non-participating dwellings shall not exceed 35 dBA. Among other things, the law also prohibits wind energy facilities from causing interference to radio, television, or internet reception on adjoining properties; requires developers to file insurance policies, acoustics expert reports, and financial security documentation at least 30 days before commencing construction; and requires developers to publish notice of the project at least once per week, for two consecutive weeks, within 30 days before filing the permit application.

    Ark. Code Ann. § 23-18-1401 et seq. (Act 945, 2025), https://arkleg.state.ar.us/Bills/Detail.

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Wind Catcher Energy Connection Project (Washington County)

    In July 2018, American Electric Power abandoned plans to build a $4.5 billion, 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle, as well as an associated interstate transmission project that would have delivered electricity to Arkansas and other states. In Arkansas, a dark money group called Protect Our Pocketbooks paid for television advertisements claiming that Arkansas would receive no benefits from the project. The developer responded by issuing a statement that Protect Our Pocketbooks was “presenting misleading information to the public, including manipulation of statements by Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson.” The developer further noted that the group “does not reveal the names of its backers or the sources of its substantial funding.” Although the Arkansas Public Service Commission ultimately granted approval for the Arkansas components of the project, the Wind Catcher project was canceled altogether when the Texas Public Service Commission (PSC) denied approval.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Nimbus Wind Farm (Carroll County)

    In 2016, Scout Clean Energy began negotiating contracts with landowners for the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm, which would cover 14 square miles of land atop the Ozark Mountains. In 2023, a group called Stop Wind Farms was formed to oppose this development and collected over 1,000 verified signatures in opposition, raising concerns about disturbances to the aesthetic value of the Ozark ridgeline and decreased property values. Nevertheless, on September 17, 2024, the Carroll County Quorum Court approved Scout to use county roads for installation, so long as Scout covered the cost for road maintenance around the wind farm. The project is expected to commence construction in 2025.

California

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. However, developers of projects meeting certain size thresholds may opt-in to a state siting process, which is administered by the California Energy Commission (CEC). The CEC has jurisdiction to issue a certificate for any: (a) photovoltaic solar facility, on-shore wind facility, or thermal energy facility not powered by fossil fuels or nuclear fuels, with a generating capacity of at least 50 megawatts (MW); (b) energy storage system with a storage capacity of least 200 MW hours (MWh); (c) electric transmission line from any such generating or storage facility to an interconnected transmission system; and (d) facility that manufactures, produces, or assembles wind, solar, or storage systems with a capital investment of at least $250,000,000 over a period of 5 years. The issuance of a certificate by the CEC eliminates the need for “any permit, certificate, or similar document required by any state, local, or regional agency,” and “supersede any applicable statute, ordinance, or regulation of any state, local, or regional agency.”

The CEC must conduct multiple public hearings of differing scope and scale before issuing a certificate. The CEC must make a final decision on the certificate within 270 days of an application being filed.

 

Cal. Pub. Res. Code §§ 25545, 25545.1, 25545.4, 25545.7, 25545.7.2, 25545.7.6, 25545.13, Cal. Gov. Code §65000 et seq.

  • BW-IDEOL Offshore Wind Project (Santa Barbara County)

    In 2022, local conservation groups and members of the Northern Chumash Tribe mobilized to oppose the proposed 40-MW BW-IDEOL Vandenberg Space Force Base Pilot offshore wind project off the coast of Santa Barbara County, which would have consisted of four floating turbines. The project site is in an area the Northern Chumash Tribe have sought to designate as a Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary. The company withdrew its lease application in February 2023.

  • Calico Solar Project (San Bernardino County)

    In 2005, Stirling Energy Systems signed a contract with a utility to sell up to 850 MW of energy from a concentrating solar-thermal power plant that would involve 30,000 solar dishes standing up to 40 feet high in the Mohave Desert. Due to concerns about impacts on the desert tortoise, project plans were reduced to 663.5 MW. In 2012, the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, and Defenders of Wildlife filed a lawsuit to stop the project, arguing that the project was “wrong from the start,” due to impacts on wild lands and wildlife. By 2013, the project was dead.

At an August 2023 meeting planned by project advocates to answer community questions, local political and environmental leaders expressed strong opposition to the project.     In 2025, D.E. Shaw Renewables proposed the 200-MW Coyote Creek Solar project which will have an additional 100 MW of battery energy storage and incorporate sheep grazing. The project is to be located on approximately 2,700 acres. In November 2025, the Sacramento Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the project after five hours of debate and testimony from over 150 speakers. Dozens of attendees spoke in opposition and raised concerns about the project’s impact on the region’s native oak tree forests, grasslands, and wetlands. The developer estimated that the project would generate approximately $76 million in tax revenue over the next 20 years and made conservation commitments including at least 1,150 acres of oak woodland, riparian habitat and wildlife corridors.

  • E-Group Solar (San Bernardino County)

    In December 2025, E-Group PS proposed the 50-MW E-Group Solar project to be located on 477 acres of land in the City of Twentynine Palms. The City enacted a ban on commercial solar facilities, which was preempted by Assembly Bill 205 (AB 205), a state law that went into effect in June 2022. AB 205 allows the developer of a solar project at least 50 MW or more to seek approval from the California Energy Commission (CEC) and bypass any local approval process. The developer opted to seek approval from the City.

    At a public meeting on February 17, 2026, the City of Twentynine Palms’ Planning Commission considered adopting a resolution recommending the City Council approve a number of amendments to the General and Development Plans to establish the renewable energy land use designation that would allow the construction of the project. During the meeting, 18 of 22 local residents in attendance voiced opposition to the project, citing concerns about potential damage to the city’s vistas, excessive dust caused by grading, and impacts to the quality of life for residents and tourists. The Planning Commission moved to continue the discussion at a future meeting and ultimately decided to transfer its decision-making authority to the City Council. On March 23, 2026, the City Council held a public hearing and after a lengthy public comment session and discussion, it denied the project in a 3-1 vote, with one abstention.

  • Fountain Wind Project (Shasta County)

    In October 2021, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors upheld the Shasta County Planning Commission’s rejection of a permit application for the Fountain Wind Project, a 4,500-acre, 200-MW wind farm proposed by Repsol. The project has faced significant opposition from the community and from the Pit River Tribe, whose ancestral homelands are within the project area. In denying the appeal, supervisors emphasized (a) the height and visibility of the turbines and (b) the potential that the presence of turbines could exacerbate the challenge of fighting wildfires. In June 2022, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 205 into law, which allowed the developer to revive the application and the California Energy Commission to consider overruling the decision. In November 2023, Shasta County and the Pit River Tribe filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the Commission from approving the project. The California Attorney General moved for a change of venue, citing possible prejudice against the California Energy Commission in the County. In April 2024, a Shasta County Superior Court judge denied the request for a change of venue but ruled that a judge from another county would preside over the lawsuit. In October 2024, the litigation was stayed. In March 2025, the California Energy Commission’s staff assessment concluded that the benefits of the project did not outweigh its environmental costs. In November 2025, the Executive Director of the California Energy Commission recommended that the state reject the approval of the project. In December 2025, the California Energy Commission unanimously denied approval of the project.

  • Genesis Solar Energy Project (Riverside County)

    The Genesis Solar Energy Project is a 250-MW concentrated solar project developed by NextEra on 1,800 acres of land near the town of Blythe in Riverside County, California. In 2010, BLM briefly halted construction on a 125-acre portion of the site that the Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) asserted was a historic crematorium, burial ground, and village for the Mojave Tribes. After the BLM found no conclusive evidence of habitation, human remains, or funerals, BLM allowed construction to resume. This led CRIT to sue NextEra in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, seeking to halt construction on the 125-acre portion. The court denied the tribe’s request for an injunction, and construction continued. Many cultural artifacts were destroyed during construction, compelling BLM to order NextEra to pay $3 million for an ethnographic study of the site and scholarship for Indigenous students.

Colorado

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over electric generating projects, including wind and solar energy projects, of any size. The local government has 120 days to decide a preliminary application, if required by the local government’s land use regulations, and 90 days to decide a final application. The Colorado Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has authority to review any denial of a project application by a local government. A certificate of public convenience and necessity is required from the CPUC for public utility facilities.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public engagement on project applications.

 

 

Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 40-5-101(3), 40-5-101, 29-20-108(5)(a), 29-20-108(2).

Connecticut

State Siting Framework

The state has principal siting authority over renewable energy projects of at least 1 megawatt (MW) in size. A certificate of environmental compatibility and public necessity (CECPN) is required from the Connecticut Siting Council for all projects that may have adverse environmental impacts, and for wind projects that are larger than 65 MW in size (regardless of their environmental impacts).

Local governments may, within 65 days of the filing of an application for a CECPN with the Connecticut Siting Council, regulate the siting of the project but any local decision may be overridden by the Council. The Appellate Court of Connecticut has held that the Connecticut Siting Council “is empowered to review decisions from [local] zoning commissions on a de novo basis, applying concerns that transcend those involved in local zoning decisions, and that review may . . . result in the approval of a particular site although the facility failed to meet the requirements of local zoning regulations.”

The Connecticut Siting Council must render a decision on an application for a CECPN within 180 days of the filing of the application. The Council is required to conduct at least 1 public hearing within 150 days from receipt of the application.

 

Conn. Gen. Stat. Ann. §§ 16-50i(a), 16-50x, 16-50x(a), 16-50k, 16-50m, 16-50p(a), 16-50x(d); Preston v. Conn. Siting Council, 20 Conn. App. 474, 483-84 (1990).

Projects with Status Pending
  • Connecticut Wind Colebrook Project (Lichfield County)

    In 2011, a community group called FairwindCT filed a lawsuit challenging the Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of BNE Energy’s petition to construct six 1.6-MW wind turbines at two separate sites in the Town of Colebrook. The trial court dismissed the lawsuit, and, in 2014, after three years of litigation, the Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the dismissal. On January 9, 2020, BNE Energy submitted a request to the Connecticut Siting Council to modify the approved plan to allow installation of a different type of wind turbine. On March 4, 2020, FairwindCT submitted an objection to the proposed modification, but the Executive Director of the Council ultimately approved the modification request. On June 1, 2020, FairwindCT and abutting landowners filed a petition with the Council for a declaratory ruling to disallow the modification. On December 17, 2020, the Council issued a final decision upholding the modification request. FairwindCT and the abutting landowners appealed to the New Britain Judicial District Superior Court, which, in November 2021, ruled in their favor, vacating the Council’s approval of the requested modification.

    CT’s First Commercial Wind Project Wins Legal Battle, Hartford Business Journal, Sept. 16, 2014, https://www.hartfordbusiness.com/article/cts-first-commercial-wind-project-wins-legal-battle; Fairwindct, Inc. v. Conn. Siting Council, 313 Conn. 669 (Feb. 21, 2014); Gold v. State Siting Council, No. HHBCV216063707, 2021 Conn Super LEXIS 1974

  • Denslow Hill Road Solar Project (New Haven County)

    In August 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council unanimously rejected a plan for a 1.5-MW solar project, citing concerns over the developer’s plans to remove about 7.9 acres of trees. In September 2024, the developer filed an appeal to the decision. In the appeal, the developer claimed that the council “exceeded” its authority, arguing that, as the owner of the land, the developer could have cleared the trees without local zoning approval and then submitted the proposal to the Siting Council, which would have had “no basis” for denying it.

Delaware

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. The Delaware Energy Office is charged with providing general support for the responsible siting of renewable energy projects but does not have final decision-making authority over projects.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the project approval process.

Del. Code Ann. tit. 29 §§ 8053, 8060, 9206.

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Florida

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects less than 75 megawatts (MW) in size. However, project developers may opt-into a state-level siting process, which is administered by the Florida Siting Board (described below).

In 2021, Florida enacted legislation preventing local governments from restricting solar energy facilities on agricultural land. The law provides that “[a] solar facility shall be a permitted use in all agricultural land use categories in a local government comprehensive plan and all agricultural zoning districts within an unincorporated area.” The law further provides that, although counties may adopt ordinances specifying buffer and landscaping requirements, any such requirements “may not exceed the requirements for similar uses involving the construction of other facilities that are permitted uses in agricultural land use categories and zoning districts.” (There is no equivalent state legislation addressing local regulation of wind facilities.)

The state has principal siting authority over solar projects larger than 75 MW. These larger projects must generally obtain a certification from the Florida Siting Board. In non-contested cases, a certification may be issued by the Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Applications for certification must be filed with the Department of Environmental Protection’s Siting Coordination Office, which has 40 days to determine if the application is complete. If the application is contested, a certification hearing must be held within 265 days of the filing of the application. Within 45 days following the hearing, a Siting Board Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) must issue a Recommended Order, indicating whether the certification should be issued and, if so, on what conditions. Following the ALJ’s recommendation, the Siting Board must issue a decision within 60 days.

Fla. Stat. Ann. §§ 163.3205(3)-(4), 403.503(14), 403.506, 403.508(f), 403.508(2)(c), 403.510, 403.508(2)(a), 403.508(5), 403.509(1)(b), 403.5066(b), 403.50663.

Georgia

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

O.C.G.A. §§ 12-7-1, 36-66-1 et seq.

Hawaii

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. A special use permit from the relevant county planning commission is required for solar projects that will occupy more than 20 acres or 10% of the parcel of land on which they are to be sited. For solar projects that will occupy more than 15 acres, approval by the Hawaii Land Use Commission is also required. Solar projects are not permitted in agricultural districts. Wind projects are allowed in agricultural districts without restrictions.

For projects requiring approval by the Hawaii Land Use Commission, the county initially reviews the project and must send its decision to the Commission, which then has 45 days to issue a decision. The county must hold at least 2 public hearings for projects to be developed on public lands. Hearings for projects on private land are at the discretion of the county.

 

HRS §§ 171-95.3, 171-95.3(c), 205-6(b), 205-2(d)(6), 205-6(e).

Idaho

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over “electric plant” projects that “facilitate the production, generation, transmission, delivery or furnishing of electricity” (including wind and solar energy projects). However, with limited exceptions, electric plant projects also require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Idaho Public Utilities Commission (IPUC). Where a CPCN is issued to a public utility, that will override any conflicting local government action or order.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for the local government or IPUC to issue a final decision on a proposed project

Idaho Code §§ 61-118, 61-119, 61-526, 67-6504, 67-6528 et seq.

Illinois

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over commercial wind and solar energy projects. However, a local government may not set standards that are more restrictive than state requirements for any commercial wind energy project that is 50 kilowatts or larger, or for any size commercial solar project.

The state requirements specify maximum setback distances, sound limitations, flicker limitations, and construction and decommissioning standards. Moreover, state law mandates that counties “may not adopt zoning regulations that disallow, permanently or temporarily, commercial wind energy facility or commercial solar energy facilities from being developed or operated in any district zones to allow agricultural or industrial uses” and “may not require permit application fees for a commercial wind energy facility or commercial solar energy facility that are unreasonable” (among other things).

The local government must hold a public hearing within 60 days of the filing of a project application and make a decision within 30 days of the public hearing.

55 ILCS §§ 5/5-12020, 5/5-12020(b), 5/5-12020(c), 5/5-12020(h), Pub. Act 102-1123 (Ill. 2023); Illinois Enacts New Law to Standardize Local Permitting for Renewable Energy Facilities, Arent Fox Schiff, Jan. 30, 2023,
https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/energy-cleantech-counsel/illinois-enacts-new-law-standardize-local-permitting.

On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further specified that, even if neighbors agreed to waive the setback requirement, any wind tower still must be at least 1,000 feet from the nearest primary structure. In 2023, Ford County amended its zoning rules to provide that, if the existing restrictions were “judicially determined to be invalid for any reason,” then the setbacks prescribed by Public Act 102-1123 (2023) would apply.

  • DeKalb County

    In 2018, DeKalb County passed an ordinance that requires wind turbines to be set back from property lines by a distance of 6 times turbine height and 3 miles from any municipality. In July 2025, the Boone County Administration Committee held a public meeting at which several local residents raised concerns over the project’s impact on property value, loss of agricultural land, and visual impacts.   • Grain Belt Express (Christian, Clark, Cumberland, Greene, Macoupin, Montgomery, Pike, Scott, and Shelby Counties)

    In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy. The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) first approved it in 2015. Landowner and agriculture groups called Concerned Citizens and Property Owners, Illinois Agricultural Association, and Landowners Alliance of Central Illinois challenged the approval in state court, and, in 2018, an Illinois appellate court overturned the approval on the grounds that regulators improperly allowed the company to use an expedited review process. The project was eventually taken over in 2020 by Invenergy, but the previous court order still prevented the project from going forward. In 2022, Gov. J.B. Pritzker signed the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which enabled construction to proceed despite the court’s ruling. The ICC approved the project for the second time in March 2023, allowing Invenergy to start building the HVDC power line. In August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on implementation of the March 2023 order to decide the project’s constitutionality. In September 2023, the court lifted the stay allowing the developer to continue with planning while the appeal moves forward. In August 2024, the Illinois appellate court reversed the ICC’s March 2023 approval of the project, citing issues with the financing of the project. In November 2024, the state’s Supreme Court granted leave to hear the appeal of the appellate court’s ruling. On July 23, 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy announced the cancellation of a $4.9 billion conditional federal loan guarantee for phase one of the project from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri. In January 2026, the Illinois Supreme Court decided the pending appeal and ruled in favor of the developer, allowing the company to move forward with construction of the project.

  • Shawnee Energy (Massac and Johnson Counties)

    In 2026, SB Energy proposed the Shawnee Energy Project, a solar energy facility, to be located on private land spanning Massac and Johnson Counties. The Johnson County Commission granted a special use permit for that County’s portion of the project, which comprises approximately 200 MW of solar generation on 1,100 acres. In February 2026, the developer submitted an application for the special use permit to the Massac County Commission for the remaining portion of the project. On February 24, 2026, the developer hosted a public meeting at the Metropolis Elks Lodge, which was attended by the Massac County Commissioners and approximately 75 local residents. During the meeting, residents opposed to the project questioned why the meeting was not held as a formal public hearing, with a question-and-answer session. The county commissioners rescheduled the meeting.

    In April 2026, the Massac County Commission held a public hearing on the project at the county courthouse. Opponents of the project raised concerns about loss of farmland, excess of stormwater runoff, and questioned the lifespan of the project and decommissioning plans. The developer stated that the footprint of the Massac County portion of the project had been reduced to 650 acres and its capacity reduced from 300 MW to 150 MW. The project is estimated to produce a total of $20 million of property taxes for Massac County over the next 25 to 35 years and create 450 jobs during construction. As of June 2026, the Massac County Commission was yet to make a decision on whether to approve the project.

  • Top Hat Wind Project (Logan County)

    As of November 2022, over 1,000 people had signed a petition opposing plans for the 200-MW, 60-turbine Top Hat Wind Project over concerns about interference with radar. That same month, however, after the developers entered into an agreement with the National Weather Service to shut off the turbines in case of severe weather, the Logan County Board approved the project. Opponents, including a group called Logan County Residents Against the Top Hat Wind Factory, stated that they were considering filing a lawsuit.

Projects with Status Operational
  • Alta Wind Farm (DeWitt County)

    The Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt County Board despite local opposition. The 200-MW project had been proposed nearly 10 years before. In October 2020, opponents filed two separate lawsuits to stop the project but dropped both of those lawsuits in March 2021. In July 2021, the DeWitt County Board approved a motion preventing the issuance of new building permits to Enel Green Power for the Alta Wind Farm until the company could prove that its turbines could be curtailed during severe weather events. An Illinois judge then issued a mandamus order holding that the Dewitt County Board lacked legal authority to halt the issuance of building permits. The wind farm proceeded to operation in June 2023.

  • HillTopper Wind Farm (Logan County)

    Considerable opposition to the construction of a 7,600-acre, 200-MW wind farm in the Mount Pulaski area led the Logan County board to initially deny the application for a conditional use permit in 2015. The project was eventually approved and was completed in 2018.

  • Niyol Wind Farm (Logan County)

    In April 2020, the Logan County Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-2 to table the conditional use permit applications for up to 82 wind turbines after a group called Concerned Citizens for a Safe Logan County expressed concerns regarding population density, sound levels and environmental protection. Despite delays caused by local opponents, the project was ultimately completed in 2021, with 74 wind turbines capable of generating 200 MW.

Indiana

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. However, state law dictates that local governments may not unreasonably restrict solar projects, except to protect public health and safety. There is no similar prohibition on local governments restricting wind projects in state law.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

Ind. Code §§ 8-1-8.5-7(2), 8-1-41-4, 8-1-42-6; 36-7-2-8; Ind. Admin. Code § 4-4.1-13.

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

    Associated Press, Wind Turbine Height Limit Set For Rural Areas Near Lafayette, WFYI, May 7, 2019, https://www.wfyi.org/news/articles/wind-turbine-height-limit-set-for-rural-areas-near-lafayette; Dave Bangert, Wind Farms Banned in Rural Tippecanoe County, as Environmentalists Grumble, Journal & Courier, May 6, 2019, https://www.jconline.com/story/news/2019/05/06/wind-farms-banned-rural-tippecanoe-county-environmentalists-grumble/3660870002/; Tippecanoe County, Ind., Unified Zoning Ordinance (3d ed.), Am. 96 (“large wind system ban”), https://www.tippecanoe.in.gov/DocumentCenter/View/24429/UZO-2022-Update-wAmendments-1-106PDF.

  • Tipton County

    Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind)
    In 2016, a few years after the opening of the divisive Wildcat Wind Farm, Tipton County amended its wind ordinance to require setbacks of 2,640 from residences and 1,500 feet from property lines.

    Carson Gerber, Howard, Tipton County Ordinances Keeping Wind Farms at Bay, Kokomo Tribune, July 17, 2016, https://www.kokomotribune.com/news/howard-tipton-county-ordinances-keeping-wind-farms-at-bay/article_0d8cfed0-4abe-11e6-8f03-c392ffe4e16e.html; Carson Gerber, “Windfall to some, a curse to many”: Tipton wind farm pays millions in taxes, but anti-wind sentiment remains, Kokomo Tribune, Sept. 14, 2020, https://www.kokomotribune.com/news/local_news/windfall-to-some-a-curse-to-many-tipton-wind-farm-pays-millions-in-taxes-but/article_3424f4c2-f45a-11ea-9623-03ed1d05dbea.html.

  • Vermillion County

    Rule 2: Capacity Cap (wind) | Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    An ordinance adopted in September 2021 requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines and roads. It further limits noise to 32 dBA at the property line and limits the size of projects in the agricultural zoning district to 100 MW.

    Vermillion County, Ind., Ordinance No. 2021-13 § 1.3 (Sep. 28, 2021), https://www.vermilliongov.us/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Wind-Energy-Conversion-Systems-Amend-to-Ordin-2021-13.pdf.

  • Wabash County

    Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind) | Rule 8: Shadow Flicker Restriction (wind)
    In 2017, Wabash County tightened its restrictions on wind development, requiring 3,960-foot setbacks from most buildings, zero shadow flicker on the properties of non-participants, and a 32-dBA limit.

    Wabash County, Ind., Ordinance No. 2017-85-9 §§ 6.24 I(I), 6.24 I(J), 6.24 R(G) (Dec. 18, 2017), http://gov.wabash.in.datapitstop.us/DATA/REPORTS/FLD00003/00007961.PDF; Wabash Plain Dealer, Wabash County Revises Wind Farm Regulation Relating to ‘Shadow Flicker’, Indiana Economic Digest, Dec. 22, 2017, https://indianaeconomicdigest.net/MobileContent/Most-Recent/Friday/Article/Wabash-County-revises-wind-farm-regulation-relating-to-shadow-flicker-/31/132/90564.

  • Wayne County

    Rule 2: Capacity Cap (wind) | Rule 9: Height Restriction (wind)
    A 2016 ordinance passed by the Wayne County Commissioners provides that large wind energy systems with a capacity greater than 50 kW or a total height of more than 100 feet are “not a permitted use.” While the ordinance sets out a procedure for small wind energy systems to obtain permission as special exceptions, the ordinance does not appear to provide a similar procedure for large systems.

    Wayne County, Ind., Zoning Ordinance § 54.76(D) (2019), https://www.co.wayne.in.us/web/dept/planpermits/WayneCountyZoningOrdinance2019-012.pdf; Mickey Shuey, Commissioners vote to limit wind farms in Wayne County, Indiana Economic Digest, Dec. 8, 2016, https://indianaeconomicdigest.net/MobileContent/Most-Recent/Wabash/Article/Commissioners-vote-to-limit-wind-farms-in-Wayne-County/31/238/86212.

  • Wells County

    Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind)
    The Wells County Zoning Ordinance, last updated in November 2022, prohibits “large” wind energy conversion systems throughout the county. The ordinance defines “large” turbines as those with more than 100 KW of peak generation capacity.

    Wells County, Ind., Zoning Ordinance, art. 9-15, 18 (Nov. 9, 2022), https://www.dropbox.com/s/ed77ef8erw1yiaf/Official%20-%20APCMEO%20WCZFMO%20WCSCO%20WCFDPO%20(11-09-2022).pdf?e=1&dl=0.

  • Whitley County

    Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind)
    Whitley County requires setbacks from property lines equal to 6.5 times the height of the tower or 2,640 feet, whichever is greater.

    Whitley County, Ind., Zoning Ordinance, ch. 5 WECS-02(E)(2) (2016), https://www.whitleygov.com/egov/documents/1439231634_83082.pdf (last visited Feb. 8, 2023); Christopher Stephens, Wind farm foe rezones to fight back, The Herald Bulletin, July 17, 2016, https://www.heraldbulletin.com/news/local_news/wind-farm-foe-rezones-to-fight-back/article_8d398421-ac87-5020-8c23-3a73eac099cd.html.

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Aypa Solar Project (Jefferson County)

    In September 2024, the Madison City Council voted to deny a rezoning proposal that would have allowed the proposed Aypa Power solar farm to proceed in Madison, Indiana. Residents expressed concerns about buffer zones and impacts on the environment and wildlife.

    City council votes against solar farm in Madison, Indiana, WHAS11, 2024, https://www.whas11.com/article/news/local/indiana/city-council-votes-against-solar-farm-madison-indiana/417-12ca7ee5-44ee-4e73-9372-6e2a72567afb; Zoning denied for proposed solar farm, TAXNOT, 2024, https://taxnot.com/zoning-denied/.

  • Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm (Henry County)

    The Henry County Planning Commission rejected a proposal for the Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm in 2019 amidst community opposition to the project. Residents raised concerns about health impacts and property rights, arguing that a 1,500-foot setback from homes was not sufficient.

    Mike Hughlett, Company Answering to Wind Farm Noise Complaints in Faribault County, Star Tribune, Feb. 17, 2018, https://www.startribune.com/company-answering-to-wind-farm-noise-complaints-in-faribault-county/474334503.

  • BrightNight Solar Project (Clark County)

    In October 2023, the Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a special exemption permit for a 3,900-acre solar project proposed by developer BrightNight. The permit was necessary because the project would have been built on agricultural land. Residents opposed the project on the basis of potential impacts to viewsheds. In 2025, the developer re-submitted the application for the project with a modified plan for developing only 1,500 acres and expanding the setbacks from 150 feet to 650 feet. At a public meeting on June 18, 2025 the Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) reached a stalemate, voting 2-2 on the application. On August 20, 2025, the project was rejected by the BZA in a 3-2 vote.

    Jose Alonzo, Clark County rejects solar farm plans in tight board vote; ‘I think it’s the right action’, WHAS11, Aug. 20, 2025, https://www.whas11.com/article/tech/science/environment/clark-county-solar-farm-proposal-rejected/417-7fbbe0b4-7b60-408c-aa15-3d9665d1f2ba; Alexandra Goldberg, ‘You’re going to feel like you’re in a prison’ | Southern Indiana residents weigh in on new solar farm project, WASH11, Jun. 11, 2025, https://www.whas11.com/article/news/community/clark-county-new-solar-farm-project-pushback/417-f202c7ba-2242-4389-8b4d-6b69fbad1157; Jose Alonzo, ‘Neighbor against neighbor’ | Vote stalled after southern Indiana residents debated future of solar farm project, WHAS11, Jun. 18, 2025, https://www.whas11.com/article/tech/science/environment/clark-county-indiana-solar-farm-vote-stalled/417-5b3ce8db-06cb-46c3-981a-63571d98d38d; Noelle Friel, Clark County Zoning Board denies permit for 3,900 acre solar farm, Wave, Oct. 18, 2023, https://www.wave3.com/2023/10/19/clark-county-zoning-board-denies-permit-3900-acre-solar-farm/.

  • Carina Solar (Bartholomew County)

    Plans to construct the 100-MW Carina Solar project on 1,880 acres of land under Bartholomew County and City of Columbus jurisdiction encountered opposition from a local group Nonprofit Bartholomew County Citizens Concerned about Commercial Solar Fields (B4CSF). In February 2024, the Bartholomew County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a conditional use permit for the 1,100-acre piece the project that would be sited within its jurisdiction. That same month, the City of Columbus Board of Zoning Appeals approved an application for a separate 800 acres piece. The developer filed a lawsuit appealing the county’s denial, while local opponents filed a lawsuit appealing the city’s approval. The Bartholomew Circuit Court consolidated the two lawsuits in June. On July 30, 2024, the developer withdrew its application as part of a stipulation dismissing the litigation

    Staff Reports, Carina Solar Farm Proposal Withdrawn, Lawsuit Dismissed, The Republic, Aug. 3, 2024, https://www.therepublic.com/2024/08/03/carina-solar-farm-proposal-withdrawn-lawsuit-dismissed/; Brad Davis, Appeals Board Votes Against Solar Proposal, The Republic, Feb. 28, 2024, https://www.therepublic.com/2024/02/28/appeals-board-votes-against-solar-proposal/.

  • Cold Spring Solar Farm (Putnam County)

    In September 2023, following fourteen months of negotiations, the Putnam County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a motion for a special exception to permit the 200-MW Cold Spring Solar Farm in Russell Township. The decision was largely based on the project’s planned utilization of 1,400 acres of farmland, and the decision received support from residents seeking to preserve the Township’s rural character.

    Jared Jernagan, Solar proposal goes dark with BZA, Banner Graphic, Sept. 13, 2023, https://www.bannergraphic.com/story/3009746.html

  • Flat Rock Wind Project (Rush County)

    In May 2015, the Rush County Board of Zoning Appeals included in a special exemption permit for the Flat Rock Wind Project the condition that all turbines be set back 2,300 feet from non-participating properties. The setback requirement exceeded the local zoning ordinances’ standard 1,000-foot setback requirement. The applicant challenged the condition in state court, and, in 2017, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld the Board of Zoning Appeals’ decision. The developer abandoned the project in December 2018, citing delays in obtaining approvals caused by local opposition and zoning disputes.

    James Sprague, Area wind project dealt huge blow, News Examiner, June 2, 2016, https://www.windaction.org/posts/45134-area-wind-project-dealt-huge-blow#.V1Wb0VfrjQA; Apex halts plans for controversial Flat Rock wind project, Fox59, Dec. 21, 2018, https://fox59.com/news/apex-halts-plans-for-controversial-flat-rock-wind-project/.

  • Hamilton County Wind (Hamilton County)

    In December 2019, the Hamilton County Board of Commissioners rejected plans for a 4-turbine, 11-MW project by Hamilton County Wind. In rejecting the plan, one commissioner noted that he believed the company had not met its burden of demonstrating that the wind farm would not pose a threat to human health. At a public hearing earlier in the month, a large crowd of opponents raised concerns including health impacts and property values.

    On December 9, 2024, the Marshall County Board of Zoning Appeals rejected plans by Invenergy to construct the 150-MW Tamarack Solar Energy Center, which would occupy 1,500 acres of land in Union Township. Local opponents raised concerns about impacts to community character.

    In 2015, NextEra proposed a 98-turbine wind farm in Rush, Henry, and Fayette Counties. By 2019, NextEra had abandoned plans for the Rush and Henry County portions and was considering a smaller 52-turbine project in Fayette County alone.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Crossvine Solar Project (Dubois County)

    In 2023, AES proposed the Crossvine Solar Project, which includes 85 MW of solar energy generation and a 85-MW battery energy storage system (BESS), to be developed on approximately 437 acres of privately owned land south of the City of Huntingburg near the Town of Holland. On November 10, 2025, during a Huntingburg City Council public meeting, residents raised concerns about the project, particularly the potential fire risk associated with BESS and the capacity of local emergency responders. The concerned residents collected over 200 signatures in opposition to the project and demanded the Council to impose a moratorium on the construction of the BESS component of the project. The Huntingburg City Mayor also expressed his opposition to large-scale solar development in the area. In response, Council officials indicated they will consult with the city attorney and hold future public meetings to continue the discussions and address the residents’ concerns.

    Matthew Crane, Residents demand moratorium on proposed solar and battery storage project,  Dubois County Free Press, Nov. 11, 2025, https://duboiscountyfreepress.com/residents-demand-moratorium-on-proposed-solar-and-battery-storage-project/; Ian Young, Huntingburg community raises concerns on potential solar project, Tristate Homepage, Nov. 10, 2025, https://www.tristatehomepage.com/news/huntingburg-community-raises-concerns-on-potential-solar-project/; AES, Crossvine Solar Project, https://www.aes.com/energy-projects/crossvine-solar-project (last visited November 24, 2025).

  • Jordan Creek Wind Energy Center (Benton and Warren Counties)

    This 400-MW project in Benton and Warren Counties began commercial operation in December 2020 despite having faced intense local opposition. Projects with Status Unknown
  • Mammoth Solar Project (Pulaski ad Starke Counties)

    Plans for a $1.5 billion, 1,300-MW solar project have encountered opposition from a resident group called Pulaski County Against Solar. Opponents have focused on the amount of agricultural land involved in the 13,000-acre project, which would include 2,600 acres of solar panels. A group of landowners filed a lawsuit to stop the project, alleging that the Pulaski County Board of Zoning Appeals’ decision granting a special exception for the project was improper because the developer’s application was incomplete. On August 24, 2021, the Indiana trial court ruled in favor of the petitioners, and, on September 21, 2022, the Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed. In July 2024, residents proposed a solar moratorium, claiming that the Mammoth project was missing important documents in the permitting process. The Starke County Commission confirmed that the documents were not missing and denied the proposed solar moratorium.

Iowa

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects that are less than 25 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of larger projects (25 MW or larger). A certificate of public convenience, use, and necessity from the Iowa Utilities Board is required for these larger facilities. State law provides that “[t]he failure of a facility to meet zoning requirements” established by cities or counties “shall not preclude the board from issuing the certificate.”

A public hearing is required on certificate applications submitted to the Utilities Board. There is no statutory deadline for the Iowa Utilities Board to issue a final decision on certificate applications.

Iowa Code §§ 335, 414, 476A.1(5), 476A.2(1), 476A.5(3), 476A.8, 476A.4; Jenna Greene, Brian Ross & Jessi Wyatt, Great Plains Inst., Siting Utility-Scale Solar and Wind in Iowa: A Guide for Local Governments, at 8 (2020)
https://betterenergy.org/wpcontent/uploads/2020/03/Solar_and_Wind_in_Iowa_Siting_Guide.pdf.

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Arbor Hill Wind Farm (Madison County)

    In August 2018, the Madison County Coalition for Scenic Preservation challenged Madison County’s decision to approve this 52-turbine wind farm. In June 2019 the district court dismissed the case and the plaintiffs appealed; the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court in January 2021. However, in December 2020, Madison County adopted an ordinance capping the number of turbines in the county at the current number, effectively preventing the project from proceeding. In January 2021, MidAmerican sued the county, and in March 2022, the parties reached a settlement allowing the company to construct 30 turbines. However, in July 2022, MidAmerican abandoned plans to move forward with the project, due to the reduction in size, among other issues.

  • Fairbank Wind Farm (Fayette County)

    A 3-turbine wind farm that was approved in 2015 and then constructed was taken down in 2018 following a successful legal challenge by residents. On appeal, the Court of Appeals of Iowa affirmed the judgment of the Iowa District Court for Fayette County that wind turbines were not “electrical and natural gas transmission and regulating facilities” within the meaning of the relevant county ordinance and thus a special permit was required for them to be placed on agricultural land.

    Mitchell Schmidt, Wind turbines haven’t been universally welcomed by everyone in Iowa, The Gazette, Feb. 23, 2019, https://www.thegazette.com/business/wind-turbines-havent-been-universally-welcomed-by-everyone-in-iowa/; Woods v. Fayette Cty. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 913 N.W.2d 275 (Iowa Ct. App. Feb. 21, 2018).

  • Mason Wind Project (Black Hawk, Buchanan, and Fayette Counties)

    In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project. The decision effectively ended plans for the project in Black Hawk County, which would have been the county’s first wind farm. Roughly fifty project opponents attended the board’s meeting and expressed concerns about potential impacts to wildlife, livestock, property values, and human health. Optimum then sought to build the project in the neighboring Buchanan County. The project also met local opposition in Buchanan County, where residents expressed concerns about the project’s potential impacts to local livelihoods and voiced skepticism about promises made by project advocates. In August 2015, the Buchanan County Planning and Zoning Commission denied a rezoning application that would have allowed Optimum Renewables to build a wind farm in the county. The project was finally built in Fayette County in 2016. Opposition continued from Fayette residents, including the group Fairbank Citizens Against Industrial Wind Turbines Near Our City, who claimed that the project violated county zoning laws. In November 2016, an Iowa judge held that the project was illegal and void due to zoning violations, issuing an order requiring its removal. In May 2018, the Iowa Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of the decision, effectively ending the project.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Coggon Solar (Linn County)

    Beginning in 2019, the developer of Coggon Solar began public outreach related to an application for a 640-acre, 100-MW solar project in Linn County. After residents voiced opposition to taking farmland out of commission, the Planning & Zoning Commission voted to recommend that the County Board of Supervisors deny the project. In January 2022, the Board voted 2-1 to approve the project. However, a family who lives near the proposed project brought a lawsuit against the board of supervisors, and, in July 2022, the Iowa Utilities Board denied Coggon Solar’s request for a certificate while the lawsuit was ongoing. On or before February 1, 2023, the court dismissed the lawsuit against the board of supervisors, paving the way for the project to move forward.

  • Siouxland Wind Farm (Woodbury County)

    The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet. As described above, the ordinance reduced the buildable acres in the county from 177 to 1.7. Opponents of the project cited noise and visual impacts, and over 700 residents signed a petition to increase the setback distance. Opponents of the project are seeking further changes to the ordinances regulating wind turbines, up to and including a ban on wind farms, and have stated that “[MidAmerican] just need[s] to pack up and go somewhere else where it’s more suitable.” MidAmerican is still looking to move forward with this project despite heavy resistance and ordinance changes.

Projects with Status Operational
  • Shenandoah Hills Wind Project (Page County)

    In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements. Just over a month after the approval, residents opposed to the project filed a lawsuit against the county and board in state court, which was later removed to federal court. In February 2023, after the developer, Invenergy, informed the Board of Supervisors that it would be removing 3 turbines from the plan, the Page County Zoning Administrator informed the developer that this was a “material change,” which rendered the application “void” and revoked the permit. The developer appealed the Zoning Administrator’s decision to the Page County Board of Adjustment. In March 2023, the Board of Adjustment upheld the revocation of the permit. A week later, the developer filed a lawsuit against the County officials in federal court challenging the revocation. In May 2024, the federal court denied the residents’ state claims which had been rendered moot at the time the permit was revoked. In November 2024, in a 2-1 vote, the Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to enter into a settlement agreement resolving the pending litigation and allowing the developer to proceed with construction of the project. In November 2025, construction of the project was completed, and the facility began operating with a total of 54 wind turbines and a generating capacity of 214 MW.

Kansas

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 12-741, 66-104(e).

State-Level Restrictions

Restrictions with Status In effect
  • Kansas Tallgrass Heartland Wind Moratorium

    Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (wind)
    In 2004, Kansas Governor Kathleen Sebelius instated a wind development moratorium on parts of the Flint Hills in order to protect the tallgrass prairie. In 2011, Governor Sam Brownback doubled the protected area, renaming it the “Tallgrass Heartland.” This moratorium, which covers parts of 12 counties, was continued in July 2020 by Governor Laura Kelly.

    State of Kansas Proclamation by the Governor, July 28, 2020, https://governor.kansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/20200728140630901.pdf. Chad Frey, Kelly reaffirms wind moratorium, The Kansan, July 30, 2020, https://www.patriotledger.com/story/news/2020/07/30/kelly-reaffirms-wind-moratorium/114905584/.

  • Acciona Barton County Solar Project (Barton County)

    Local community members opposed a proposed 300-MW solar project near Cheyenne Bottoms, the largest inland wetland in the United States. As of February 2023, there are no Calpine projects in Kansas or public plans to build in Anderson County.

    In 2023, Evergy proposed the Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project, a 159-MW solar farm to be developed on approximately 1,103 acres in Grant Township near Lawrence, Kansas. The project developer sought a conditional use permit from the Douglas County Planning Commission. The Commission received approximately 50 comments on the project, 30 of which expressed opposition to it. Voices against the project focused on the need to preserve agricultural land. In December 2023, the Douglas County Planning Commission’s review ended in a split 4-4 vote on the permit application. In April 2024, the Commission unanimously voted to approve the conditional use permit. In May 2024, a group of opponents of the project brought a lawsuit in the Douglas County District Court alleging that the approval of the permit conflicts with the County’s comprehensive plan and solar regulations. In December 2024, the District Court Judge issued an injunction preventing any construction on the project until the litigation is resolved. In October 2025, the Douglas County Commissioners voted unanimously to approve five temporary business use permits (TBUs) allowing the developer to conduct environmental testing for the project subject to a number of conditions while the litigation remains pending.

Kentucky

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over energy generation projects, including wind and solar energy projects, that are less than 10 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of larger energy generation facilities  (10 MW or more). These larger projects require a construction certificate from the Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation but are still subject to local zoning ordinances.

The State Board must make a decision on a certificate application within 120 days of receipt or 180 days if a hearing is requested. The applicant is required to hold a public meeting prior to filing a certificate application. The State Board must also convene a public hearing upon the request of 3 or more local residents or certain local officials.

Ky. Rev. Stat. §§ 278.700, 278.704, 278.704(4), 278.706(2)(f), 278.710, 278.712(1).

Louisiana

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that will occupy less than 75 acres of land. A permit from the Louisiana Department of Energy and Natural Resources (DENR) is required for solar facilities that will occupy 75 or more acres of land, with certain exceptions for facilities owned by electric utilities. A permit from the DENR is also required for all onshore wind facilities.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local governments or the state DENR to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

La. R.S. §§ 33:106, 33:109, 30:1131 and 1141 through 1145, 30.1154(A), 30.1154(D).

Projects with Status Pending
  • White Castle Solar Farm (Iberville and Pointe Coupee Parishes)

    Developer NextEra has proposed a 2,057-acre solar project in Iberville and Pointe Coupee Parishes. Pointe Coupee Parish residents have generally not opposed the project, but a contingent in Iberville Parish has stood in strong opposition to it. Citing concerns about devalued property, loss of farmland, and impacts to the parishes’ rural atmosphere, project opponents held up signs saying “no solar” and “you’re not wanted here” at a September 2023 parish meeting. Parish President Mitchell Ourso voiced his opposition to the project, saying, “I cannot support this project here in our parish. . . . Before there was industry in our parish, everything was agriculture. This has no economic impact, and I think it can be detrimental for years to come in White Castle.”

Maine

State Siting Framework

All wind and solar energy projects must be approved by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). Solar energy projects require the following permits from the DEP: a stormwater permit if the project will occupy 20 acres or less; a permit under the Site Location of Development Act if the project is larger than 20 acres; and a Natural Resources Protection Act permit if the project will be sited near protected natural resources.

Wind project permitting differs depending on the size and location of the project. Grid-scale wind projects that are to be developed outside an expedited permitting area require a permit from the DEP under the Site Location of Development Act. A public hearing must generally be held on permit applications, but that requirement can be waived in certain circumstances. Before issuing a permit, the DEP must determine that the project meets applicable standards including with respect to noise mitigation, stormwater management, and protection of groundwater, wildlife and fisheries, and natural areas.

Grid-scale wind projects to be located within an expedited permitting area identified by the Maine Land Use Planning Commission and small-scale wind projects (non-grid-scale later 0.1 megawatts) that are proposed outside of an expedited permitting area are regulated under the Maine Energy Act. Under the Maine Energy Act, the DEP must certify that the wind development will meet the noise control requirements adopted by the Board of Environmental Protection, will be designed and sited to avoid unreasonable adverse shadow flicker effects, and will be constructed with setbacks adequate to protect public safety as recommended by a licensed civil engineer and by a manufacturer of the generating facility.

The DEP must issue a decision on permit applications for wind projects in expedited permitting areas within 185 days of accepting the application, or within 270 days if a public hearing is held.

38 M.R.S.A. §§ 341-D(2), 480-II, 480-B(8), 481-490, 482(2), 482-6-B, 488, 489-A-1, 3451(8), 3456, 4352(6), 3471-3474; 06 C.M.R. ch. 2, § 096-2-13; 35-A M.R.S.A. §§ 3451(8), 3456.

State-Level Restrictions

Restrictions with Status In effect
  • Maine Bill L.D. 1619 of 2021

    Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (wind)
    In July 2021, Governor Janet Mills signed into law L.D. 1619, sponsored by Senator Mark Lawrence. With some exceptions, the law permanently banned the development of all offshore wind projects in Maine state waters but allowed the permitting of offshore wind in federal waters if the Governor’s Energy Office developed a planned research strategy for such projects by March 2023. The law also created the Offshore Wind Research Consortium (ORWC) to study the effects of offshore wind energy on the Gulf of Maine. The law was supported by Maine lobstermen, who expressed concerns about the impact of offshore wind on the state’s fishing industry.

    Maine P.L. 2021 c. 407; Nick Linder, Mills sign offshore wind ban amid lingering skepticism among fishermen, Maine Wire, July 11, 2021, https://www.themainewire.com/2021/07/mills-signs-offshore-wind-ban-amid-lingering-skepticism-from-fishermen/.
