Projects with Status Pending
  • Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project (Kennebec and Waldo Counties)

    The Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and Massachusetts. LS Power was initially developing the project. In June 2023, Maine adopted a bill approving the project, but the project has been slowed by local opposition and moratoria. Maine residents opposing the project have raised concerns about impacts to property and sightlines, formed a citizen group called Preserve Rural Maine, and obtained legal counsel. In August 2023, in response to this project, the town of Albion imposed a 6-month moratorium on utility lines and corridors, with residents expressing concerns that the project would disrupt farmland and that the project’s electromagnetic fields would disorient bees. Also, in response to the project, in September 2023, the Town of Palermo adopted a transmission line moratorium. In November 2023, the Town of Unity adopted a 180-day moratorium on high-voltage power lines. In December 2023, LS Power announced that it could no longer proceed with the project at the agreed-upon price. In response, the Maine Public Utilities Commission announced that it was terminating its agreement with LS Power and delaying development until it could find another developer for the project. However, in October 2024, the Department of Energy announced a $425 million capacity contract with Avangrid to restart conversations with the Maine PUC on continuing the transmission project. In November 2024, the Town of China’s select board passed a 180-day High-Impact Electric Transmission Line Moratorium Ordinance in response to the project.

Maryland

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal authority over the siting of solar energy projects that are less than 5 megawatts (MW) in size. State law preempts local bans on solar projects that are 1 MW or larger and all energy storage projects (regardless of size).

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that are 5 MW or larger and wind projects that are 70 MW or larger in size. A certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland Public Service Commission (MPSC) is required for projects under state jurisdiction. Solar projects that are more than 5 MW but less than 25 MW in size and wind projects that are less than 70 MW in size are exempt from the CPCN requirement but still require MPSC approval.

A public hearing is required on CPCN applications. There is no statutory permitting timeline for the approval of a project application.

Renewable Energy Certainty Act of 2025, https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2025RS/bills/sb/sb0931E.pdf; Md. Code, Pub. Util. Co. §§ 3-106, 7-207, 7-207.1, 7-207.2, 7-208, 7-207.1(f); Steven Ferrey, Siting Technology, Land-Use Energized, 66 Cath. U. L. Rev. 1, 24 (2017), https://scholarship.law.edu/lawreview/vol66/iss1/6/.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Betterton Halo Solar (Kent County)

    In 2025, Halo Betterton, LLC proposed the 5-MW Betterton Halo Solar project to be located on approximately 30 acres of land in the Town of Betterton. In April 2025, the developer applied for the required Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC). In May 2025, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources recommended that the application be deemed administratively complete.

    In September 2025, the PSC held a public hearing on the project at which town officials expressed their opposition to it, citing concerns about potential impacts to the town’s residential character and public safety risks because the project site would block their designated helicopter landing zone. Nearly two dozen opponents at that hearing also raised concerns over historical preservation, public safety, and impacts on property values. In November 2025, a town community meeting was held at which over 50 local residents and representatives of regional preservation groups, including the Kent Conservation and Preservation Alliance, objected to the project, primarily on the grounds that the proposed project site is restricted to residential use. In December 2025, the PSC stayed the proceedings to review the legal question of whether the proposed project site is zoned for clean energy development.

  • Maryland Offshore Wind Project a/k/a MarWin a/k/a US Wind (Worcester County)

    The Maryland Offshore Wind Project, proposed by US Wind, has the potential to generate up to 2,200 MW. The project has encountered opposition from the Ocean City government and the tourism industry due to concerns that visual impacts will harm business. In February 2018, the Ocean City Mayor and Council unanimously approved a resolution against any wind project being sited within 30 miles of the city. The City officials proposed a similar bill in the General Assembly that would have required siting at least 26 miles off the coast, but the Maryland House of Delegates rejected the proposed legislation. In September 2021, after the developer applied for an expansion of the project size, several local elected officials and business leaders expressed concern about turbines ruining beachfront views, jeopardizing tourism, and negatively impacting real estate values and the local economy. In November 2023, Worcester County Commissioners sent a letter to the Army Corps of Engineers urging the Corps to deny a permit for US Wind. In October 2024, Ocean City and other plaintiffs, including Worcester County, various community associations, and the Ocean City Marlin Club, filed a lawsuit in federal court, alleging that the federal government’s approval of the project violated the Administrative Procedure Act, National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Coastal Zone Management Act, Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and National Historic Preservation Act. In December 2024, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management issued its final approval of the project. In January 2025, the Army Corps issued the permit for the project. In July 2025, the federal court ruled on the motions to dismiss the case by the federal defendants and the developer intervenor. While the court dismissed several of the claims, it allowed the claims under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act to proceed, and reserved judgment on the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the National Environmental Policy Act claims. In September 2025, the Department of Interior filed a motion indicating that it planned to withdraw its approval for the project and alleging that the approval process did not address potential impacts on other offshore uses, such as fishing. The litigation remains pending.

Massachusetts

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over small-scale wind and solar energy projects less than 25 megawatts (MW) in size. These projects require a  consolidated permit (including all necessary municipal, regional and state permits) from the relevant local government. The local government must make a decision whether to grant or deny the permit within 12 months of receipt of a complete permit application.

The state has principal authority over larger wind and solar projects of 25 MW or more. These larger projects require a consolidated permit from the Energy Facilities Siting Board (EFSB). The EFSB must make a decision whether to grant or deny the permit within 15 months of receipt of a completed permit application. The developer of a small-scale wind or solar project (less than 25 MW in size) may opt to seek a consolidated permit from the EFSB, though the required local permits remain under the authority of the relevant local government.

The EFSB is required to conduct a public hearing in at least 1 of the affected cities or towns in which a large wind or solar project would be located. Local governments are required to establish uniform pre-filing requirements for small-scale wind and solar projects that shall include provisions for public meetings and other forms of public engagement.

Mass. Session Laws ch. 239 of 2024; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A § 3; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164 §§ 69G, 69J1/4, 69K1/2, 69T; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 25A § 21; see also Steven Ferrey, Siting Technology, Land-Use Energized, 66 Cath. U. L. Rev. 1, 25 (2017), https://scholarship.law.edu/lawreview/vol66/iss1/6/.

  • City of Waltham (Middlesex County)

    Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar)
    The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones. A developer who owned land in Waltham and a neighboring town sought permission from the city building inspector to build an access road on the land the developer owned in Waltham to a proposed 1-MW solar facility in a neighboring town. The building inspector denied permission on the basis of local zoning restrictions. On June 4, 2022, the Supreme Judicial Court struck down the restrictions, finding that “[a]n outright ban of large-scale solar energy systems in all but one to two percent of a municipality’s land area . . . restricts rather than promotes the legislative goal of promoting solar energy” and that, “in the absence of a reasonable basis grounded in public health, safety, or welfare, such a prohibition is impermissible.” Note that this is included as a pre-March 2022 development because the relevant restriction was in place before March 2022.

    Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions.   • Town of Northfield (Franklin County)

    In May 2024, residents of Northfield voted in favor of two citizen’s petitions to place 1-year moratoriums on utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities. During the annual town meeting, proponents argued that the moratoriums would provide time for the town to draft bylaws regulating utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities. Opponents argued that the moratoriums would halt the town’s efforts toward clean energy. Some commenters noted that the moratorium might conflict with state law, as Chapter 40A, Section 3 of Massachusetts General Law states that “No zoning ordinance or bylaw shall prohibit or unreasonably regulate the installation of solar energy systems or the building of structures that facilitate the collection of solar energy, except where necessary to protect the public health, safety or welfare.”

  • Cape Wind (Barnstable County)

    In 2017, after spending $100 million of his own money, the developer of Cape Wind, a proposed 454-MW offshore wind farm, abandoned the project. For years, the project was weighed down by costly legal challenges from groups such as the Alliance to Protect Nantucket Sound. In addition to the Alliance to Protect Nantucket Sound, which was chaired by William Koch, the project faced opposition from fishing groups and Native American tribes. As a result of delays caused by opposition, Cape Wind was unable to meet the construction deadlines set out in power purchase agreements. In 2015, two utilities canceled their contracts with Cape Wind.

  • Falmouth Wind (Barnstable County)

    Two turbines known as Falmouth Wind 1 and 2, which were installed in 2010 and 2013, faced opposition from neighbors based in part on concerns about noise and health impacts. In March 2013, two residents of the Town of Falmouth filed a complaint with the Falmouth Building Commissioner alleging that two wind turbines were a nuisance. The Building Commissioner denied the request to compel the Town to shut the turbines down. However, in December 2013, after holding a public meeting, the Falmouth Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) found that the turbines were a nuisance and overturned the denial. In 2014, the Town of Falmouth, as owner and operator of the turbines, filed a lawsuit in state court against the ZBA, alleging that the ZBA’s decision to shut down the turbines was arbitrary and capricious. The court sided with the ZBA, finding that the wind turbines posed a nuisance and ordering that the turbines be permanently stopped. By October 2022, the Town had demolished the two wind turbines.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Cape Cod Solar (Barnstable County)

    In 2019, PureSky Energy proposed the Cape Cod Solar project on approximately 83 acres (out of over 200 acres) of a former country club golf course in the Town of Falmouth. The project consists of three solar facilities with battery energy storage systems (BESS) and has a total capacity of up to 13.5 MW. The project has faced opposition from local residents, who have advocated for the preservation of the golf course on the grounds that it is historically significant. A Change.org petition garnered over 3,500 signatures to preserve the nearly 100-year-old golf course. Other opponents have expressed a preference for the development of housing, rather than the solar facility, on the land. In September 2025, the Cape Cod Commission, in a 14-1 vote, approved the conversion of the golf course. In November 2025, the Town approved the site conversion plans which include donating approximately 137 acres to the town to be protected as permanent open space. The solar project will now go before the Falmouth Planning Board for site plan review.

  • New England Wind 2, formerly known as Commonwealth Wind Project and Park City Wind (Barnstable County)

    In 2017, Avangrid began the development of two offshore wind farms south of Martha’s Vineyard – Commonwealth Wind (1,200-MW) and Park City Wind (800-MW). In April 2023, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Edgartown Conservation Commission after the town denied the company’s request to install subsurface transmission cables in town waters (see separate entry for New England Wind 1). Avangrid received a favorable ruling from the court, and in September 2023, the Commission rescinded its denial of the request. At a November 2023 Town public meeting concerning offshore wind, many Barnstable residents opposed plans to bring the cable installation, expressing concerns about disruption to public beaches and roads and impacts from electromagnetic fields. The citizen group Save Greater Dowses Beach formed in opposition to Avangrid’s plans to install the cables. In December 2023, the state Energy Facilities Siting Board voted to permit the landing of underground cables for the projects at Craigville Beach in Barnstable. In April 2024, the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) reviewed and approved the projects, which were combined and rebranded as New England Wind 2. In May 2025, the group ACK for Whales filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia challenging the project alleging that the BOEM approval process violated several federal environmental laws, including the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. In September 2025, the Department of Interior filed a motion indicating that it is reconsidering its 2024 permit approval for the project. The litigation remains pending.

  • Petersham Solar (Worcester County)

    In 2021, Sunpin Energy proposed the 4.3-MW Petersham Solar project to be located on approximately 14 acres in Petersham, Worcester County. In November 2021, after four public meetings, the Petersham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) voted 2-1 to approve the developer’s application for a special use permit for the project. However, as a unanimous vote was required, the permit was not issued. The dissenting board member and local residents opposing the project, expressed concern that it would require the cross-cutting of forest in a 14-acre parcel and harm the character of the community.

    In December 2021, the developer challenged the ZBA’s decision in the Massachusetts Land Court. In August 2023, the Land Court ruled that the ZBA had acted within their authority and the denial was reasonable based on public safety, health, and welfare. The developer subsequently challenged the Land Court’s ruling in the Massachusetts Appeals Court. In July 2025, the Appeals Court reversed, holding that the proposed use was allowed with a special permit, and that the ZBA had exceeded their discretion in denying the permit. The matter is currently on appeal by the ZBA before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.

  • Vineyard Wind 1 (Nantucket County)

    In 2017, Avangrid Renewables proposed a 62-turbine, 800-MW offshore wind project located more than 15 miles of Martha’s Vineyard. The project has faced opposition from fishing industry groups, a solar developer, and a local citizen group called Nantucket Residents Against Turbines (ACKRATS). In 2021 and 2022, these groups filed four separate lawsuits against the project in federal court. All four lawsuits alleged insufficient consideration of potential impacts to right whales, among other claims. The cases include claims under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA), Clean Water Act (CWA), Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and the Merchant Marine Act of 1920. Between May and October 2023, the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts decided all four cases in favor of Vineyard Wind and the federal government. All four cases were appealed to the First Circuit. In April 2024, the First Circuit affirmed the lower court’s decision in two of the cases: Nantucket Residents Against Turbines v. U.S. Bureau of Energy Management, and Melone v. Coit. In December 2024, the First Circuit affirmed dismissal of two related lawsuits by Responsible Offshore Development Alliance (RODA) and Seafreeze Shoreside. In September 2024, Nantucket Residents Against Turbines filed a petition for certiorari in the U.S. Supreme Court. In January 2025, the certiorari petition was denied. RODA and Seafreeze subsequently filed petitions for certiorari, but those petitions were also denied in May 2025. On December 22, 2025, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) issued a stop-work order to halt construction of the project for reasons of national security. In January 2026, the developer filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts to enjoin BOEM’s stop-work order. In late January 2026, the federal district judge granted the plaintiff’s request for a preliminary injunction and allowed construction of the project to resume.

Projects with Status Unknown
  • Amherst Capped Landfill Solar (Hampshire County)

    In 2011, the Town of Amherst selected SunEdison to build a 2.4-MW solar array on a capped town landfill. In response, citizens filed a lawsuit against town officials for allegedly violating an agreement with the state that the landfill site must be used for recreational purposes. The lawsuit became moot in February 2012, when the state legislature passed a bill allowing all capped municipal landfills to serve as sites for solar projects. In April 2012, plaintiffs amended the lawsuit to include potential impacts to habitat of the grasshopper sparrow, which is protected under the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice in December 2015. However, in July 2016 town officials terminated their contract with SunEdison after learning from the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife that the landfill solar project would likely impact habitat of the grasshopper sparrow.

    Scott Merzbach, Controversial Amherst solar project abandoned, Daily Hampshire Gazette, July 8, 2016, https://www.gazettenet.com/Solar-project-on-older-capped-landfill-in-Amherst-terminated-3334840

  • Future Generation Wind (Barnstable and Plymouth Counties)

    In 2016, the Town of Bourne filed suit against Future Generation Wind, claiming that the company was failing to consider the impacts in Bourne of a 4-turbine, 6-MW wind farm it was constructing in the neighboring town of Plymouth. In February 2020, after the wind farm was constructed, the Plymouth Board of Health unanimously voted that it constituted a public nuisance. The Board had received over 360 complaints since the 500-foot turbines began operating in 2016. The Board also voted to take action against Future Generation Wind “in a reasonable amount of time,” though more information on the Board’s actions does not appear to be available.

    In September 2017, residents in the town of Savoy voted against an amendment that would have allowed Minuteman Wind LLC to extend the height of their turbines from 425 to 453 feet. The 28-foot extension would have increased the energy output by 15%. Savoy residents had expressed frustration with Minuteman Wind and the noise West Hill had created in their community.

Michigan

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts (MW) in size and wind projects less than 100 MW in size. Localities have the option to retain control over larger projects if they have adopted a “compatible renewable energy ordinance” (CREO), which is not more restrictive than applicable state law. In October 2024, the Michigan Public Service Commission (PSC) issued an order with guidance on what local governments can, and cannot, include in a CREO. That order was challenged in court in November 2024. In May 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals partially upheld the PSC’s order, but remanded key sections of it back to the PSC for further consideration.

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that 50 MW or larger in size and wind projects that are 100 MW or larger. A certificate from the Michigan PSC is required for these larger projects. The PSC may preempt local restrictions on such projects.

The PSC must determine whether a certificate application is complete within 60 days of receipt and issue a final decision within 1 year of the filing of the application. Local governments with a CREO must issue a decision on a project application within 120 days of receipt, otherwise the PSC obtains jurisdiction. A public meeting is required for projects under PSC jurisdiction.

Mich. PA 233 §§ 222, 223 (3)b, 225 (2), 226(5), 227, 232; Michigan H.B. 5120 of 2023 (effective date Nov. 29, 2024); Matthew Eisenson, Michigan Court of Appeals Considers Challenge to New Process for Siting Renewables, Climate Law Blog, Apr. 11, 2025,
https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2025/04/11/michigan-court-of-appeals-considers-challenge-to-new-process-for-siting-renewables/.

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

    In December 2019, the Sherwood Township Board voted to adopt a restrictive wind ordinance (later approved by voters in August 2020) that limits turbine height to 330 feet (approximately half the height of the tallest onshore turbines) and imposes a setback from property lines equal to 500% of tower height and additional setbacks of 0.5 miles from water, 1 mile from the Village of Sherwood, and 2 miles from environmentally sensitive areas. As with Batavia Township and Matteson Township, the restrictions were promoted aggressively on Facebook by a group called Concerned Citizens of Branch County in response to efforts by DTE Energy to develop a wind farm in the area, which was ultimately put on hold in August 2020.

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Beaver Township Wind Farm (Bay County)

    In 2018, DTE Energy canceled plans to develop a wind farm in Beaver Township after the township board “set a sound limit that was so low that it basically would not allow any turbine in any 1-mile by-1 mile section.” Opponents of the project had voiced concerns about impacts to property value and wildlife, as well as physical safety.

    Isis Simpson-Mersha, DTE says township ordinance makes wind farm project ‘impossible’, M Live Michigan, May 16, 2018, https://www.mlive.com/news/bay-city/2018/05/township_makes_it_impossible_f.html; Beaver Township, Mich., Zoning Ordinance §§ 3.24(4)(b), 3.24(4)(c), 3.25(d)(2), 3.25(d)(7), 3.25(d)(11) (Oct. 26, 2022), https://storage.googleapis.com/wzukusers/user-25065735/documents/3d57f0d79e60488aab2185a88cb343c4/Zoning%20Ordinance%202019-02%20Amended%2010-26-22.pdf.

  • Filion Wind Park (Huron County)

    In May 2017, the 70-turbine Filion Wind Park was rejected by voters in four Michigan townships through petition drives and referendum votes. The project had previously received approval from Huron County officials. In an interview, a renewable energy director from DTE Energy claimed that this and a related decision have caused DTE Energy to look elsewhere for future renewable energy projects. The secretary of the Huron County Wind Resistance, a local anti-wind energy group, responded to the news as follows: “All I can say is, the people have spoken. We didn’t persuade them any more than asking them and pleading with them to go to the polls with our big advertising dollars. But, they showed up, and they said, ‘no.’ Victory for the people is what we’re saying.”

    Andy Balaskovitz, As voters reject additional development in Michigan’s ‘wind capital,’ what next, Energy News Network, May 11, 2017, https://energynews.us/2017/05/11/as-voters-reject-additional-development-in-michigans-wind-capital-what-next/; Brenda Battel, Voters say no to more wind development, Huron Daily Tribune, May 3, 2017, https://www.michigansthumb.com/news/article/Voters-say-no-to-more-wind-development-11116608.php; Emily Le Coz & Lucille Sherman, Communities Fight Wind Farms, Face Pushback, Gatehouse Media, Dec. 13, 2017, https://stories.usatodaynetwork.com/windfarms/the-resistance/.

  • Goodland Township Solar Project (Lapeer County)

    On June 11, 2022, the Goodland Township Planning Commission voted to deny Orion Renewable Energy’s application for a special land use permit to construct a 100-MW solar farm on up to 1,600 acres of land. Commissioners said the project would not be in harmony with the township’s existing agricultural and residential uses.

    Jeff Hogan, Solar panel project in Goodland Township denied, The County Press, June 11, 2022, https://thecountypress.mihomepaper.com/articles/solar-panel-project-in-goodland-township-denied.

  • Huron Wind Energy Center (Huron and Sanilac Counties)

    The Huron Wind Energy Center was a proposed 150-MW, 60-turbine wind farm being developed by NextEra in Sherman and Sigel Townships. In May 2017, at the same time as Huron County voters rejected the Filion Wind Park through referenda votes, Huron County residents voted against a wind overlay district proposed by NextEra Energy that was necessary to construct the Huron Wind Energy Center in those townships. The project had already been approved by Huron County officials, and the May 2017 voting occurred through referendum.

    Andy Balaskovitz, As voters reject additional development in Michigan’s ‘wind capital,’ what next, Energy News Network, May 11, 2017, https://energynews.us/2017/05/11/as-voters-reject-additional-development-in-michigans-wind-capital-what-next/; Brenda Battel, Voters say no to more wind development, Huron Daily Tribune, May 3, 2017, https://www.michigansthumb.com/news/article/Voters-say-no-to-more-wind-development-11116608.php; Emily Le Coz & Lucille Sherman, Communities Fight Wind Farms, Face Pushback, Gatehouse Media, Dec. 13, 2017, https://stories.usatodaynetwork.com/windfarms/the-resistance/.

  • Iosco Solar (Livingston County)

    In 2025, DTE Energy proposed the Iosco Solar project to be located on approximately 1,800 acres of land spanning two districts zoned as agricultural land in Iosco Township. In June 2025, the Iosco Township Planning Commission recommended approval of two conditional rezoning requests needed for the project to move forward on the site. On December 18, 2025, at a Township Board public meeting, the Board unanimously denied the two rezoning requests. The denial was followed by loud applause and a standing ovation from project opponents, who had raised concerns over government overreach, loss of rural character, decreased property values, loss of farmland, noise, and public safety.

    Jessica Matthews, Iosco Township Board Denies Rezonings For Massive DTE Solar Project, WHMI, Dec. 18, 2025, https://www.whmi.com/news/article/iosco-board-denies-rezonings-dte-solar.

  • Kenowa Ridge Wind Farm (Kent and Muskegon County)

    In December 2019, American Electric Power canceled plans to build 31 wind turbines in two Michigan townships after one of those townships, Casnovia, adopted a restrictive ordinance that requires wind turbines to be set back from property lines by a distance of 4 times turbine height. Casnovia Township had previously approved a special use permit for the wind farm in April 2019 and was sued by local residents opposed the project; the developer also sued Casnovia Township alleging that the permit included 32 “capricious and arbitrary” conditions that would make it impossible to build the project.

    Ben Solis, Energy company nixes planned wind farm east of Muskegon, M Live Michigan, Dec. 24, 2019, https://www.mlive.com/news/muskegon/2019/12/energy-company-nixes-planned-wind-farm-east-of-muskegon.html.

  • Meade Wind Farm (Huron County)

    DTE canceled plans to construct a 100-MW wind farm in Meade Township after the project was rejected by residents in a May 2015 referendum, which overturned Meade Township Board’s November 2013 approval of the project.

    Kelly Krager, Oliver Twp. Planners OK DTE wind park plan, Huron County View, Aug. 10, 2015, https://huroncountyview.mihomepaper.com/articles/oliver-twp-planners-ok-dte-wind-park-plan.

  • Pegasus Wind (Tuscola County)

    In June 2019, Pegasus Wind applied for zoning variances to construct 33 wind turbines near a local airport. The Tuscola Airport Zoning Board of Appeals (AZBA) denied the applications for variances, citing concerns about air traffic safety. The developer appealed the denials to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which reversed the AZBA’s decision. In October 2019, Pegasus Wind submitted applications for 8 additional variances, which the AZBA again denied. Pegasus Wind appealed the denial to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which affirmed the denial. In 2022, the Michigan Court of Appeals reversed the Circuit Court’s decision, finding that denial was improper. However, in April 2024, the Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals’ decision, allowing the AZBA’s denial of the variances to stand.

    Pegasus Wind, LLC v. Tuscola County, 511 Mich. 977 (2024), https://www.courts.michigan.gov/49699b/siteassets/case-documents/opinions-orders/msc-term-opinions-%28manually-curated%29/23-24/pegasus-wind-op.pdf.

  • Portside Solar (St. Clair County)

    In November 2023, Fort Gratiot Township commissioners unanimously rejected a 900-acre solar project, resulting in applause from residents attending the commissioner meeting. At the meeting and in written comments, residents opposed to the Portside Solar project raised concerns pertaining to potential noise, environmental impacts, and impacts to agricultural land.

    Jackie Smith, ‘Disruptive’ to farmland? Fort Gratiot commission rejects 900-acre solar project, Times Herald, Nov. 9, 2023, https://thetimesherald.com/story/news/2023/11/09/disruptive-to-farmland-fort-gratiot-commission-rejects-900-acre-solar-project/71515046007/.

  • Sandstone Creek Solar Project (Eaton County)

    In 2016, National Grid Renewables, formerly known as Geronimo Energy, doing business as Sandstone Creek, LLC (“Sandstone”), proposed a 65-MW solar project in Benton Township. In October 2019, Sandstone acquired permits and property interests in 850 acres of land after the county amended its Land Development Code to facilitate the project. In November 2019, the Benton Township Board of Trustees adopted a resolution in opposition to the project, Solar Farm Resolution 2017-2, which imposed a moratorium on solar permits and zoned the land exclusively for agricultural use. This effectively barred the development. Sandstone sought injunctive relief in state court. The trial court and court of appeals denied the injunction, concluding that the Board of Trustees sufficiently followed the procedures of the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act.

    Sandstone Creek Solar, LLC v. Twp. of Benton, 335 Mich. App. 683 (Mich. Ct. App., February 4, 2021).

  • Scandia Wind (Mason, Muskegon, Oceana and Ottawa Counties)

    In 2009, Scandia Wind began proposing to develop an offshore wind farm consisting of 100 to 200 turbines in Lake Michigan. The proposal generated significant opposition. The developer offered to reduce the scale of the project and move it farther offshore and then abandoned the proposal altogether.

    Nicole Pollack, What happened to the Great Lakes Offshore Wind Boom?, Inside Climate News, Nov. 24, 2023, https://insideclimatenews.org/news/24112023/what-happened-to-the-great-lakes-offshore-wind-boom/; Whatever happened to offshore wind energy? Five years since Lake Michigan wind turbines proposed, Michigan Live, Feb. 11, 2015, https://www.mlive.com/news/muskegon/2015/02/whatever_happened_to_offshore.html.

  • Summit Lake Wind Project (Baraga County)

    In April 2019, Renewable Energy Systems canceled plans for a proposed 49-turbine wind farm in L’Anse Township, Baraga County. The project faced opposition from a local group called Friends of the Huron Mountains. After the L’Anse Township Board approved an amendment to the zoning ordinance supported by the developer, which would have allowed wind turbines on commercial forest land, opponents forced a referendum to overturn the amendment. The project was abandoned before the referendum was held.

    Benjamin Raven, Company cancels plans for wind farm with 49 turbines in Michigan’s UP, M Live Michigan, Apr. 22, 2019, https://www.mlive.com/news/2019/04/company-cancels-plans-for-wind-farm-with-49-turbines-in-michigans-up.html.

Projects with Status Pending
  • 45th Parallel Solar (Otsego County)

    RWE Clean Energy proposed a 200-MW solar farm, called 45th Parallel Solar, to be developed on approximately 1,000 acres of private land in Hayes Township. In February 2025, the Otsego County Planning Commission, in a 7-1 vote, approved a special use permit for the project. The developer had submitted a separate proposal to lease additional public land for the project. In May 2025, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources rejected the leasing proposal following mass public criticism from both lawmakers and environmental organizations, citing concerns over deforestation and a lack of transparency. The development of the project continues on the proposed 1,000 acres of private land and commercial operations are estimated to begin in 2027.

    45th Parallel Solar, RWE, https://americas.rwe.com/our-energy/solar-energy/solar-projects-and-locations/45th-parallel-solar/ (last visited September 9, 2025); Sheldon Krause, Northern Michigan counties approve solar projects, boosting renewable energy efforts,9&10 NEWS, Aug. 11, 2025, https://www.9and10news.com/2025/08/11/northern-michigan-counties-approve-solar-projects-boosting-renewable-energy-efforts/; Keith Matheny, DNR halts state land leases for utility-scale solar projects, DETROIT FREE PRESS, May 23, 2025, https://www.freep.com/story/news/local/michigan/2025/05/23/dnr-halts-state-land-leases-utility-scale-solar-projects/83794371007/; Otsego County Planning Commission, Meeting Minutes, February 3, 2025, https://www.otsegocountymi.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Minutes/_02032025-1171.

  • Birch Valley Solar (Tuscola County)

    Ranger Power has proposed to construct a 170-MW solar facility called Birch Valley Solar on approximately 1,500 acres of farmland in Arbela Township. If completed, the project would net $340,000 annually for the township’s fire, infrastructure, or safety expenses. The proposal also includes a host community agreement requiring the developer to pay the township $2,000 per MW of installed capacity. Despite the anticipated benefits, the project is facing local opposition. Opponents have raised concerns of encroachment on prime farmland and the fact that the project’s scale would exceed the local zoning ordinance’s cap on utility-scale solar development of 4% of total township acreage. In July 2025, the developer submitted an application for a special land use permit. If the Arbela Township Board of Trustees denies the permit, the developer may seek project approval from the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) under the Public Act 233 of 2023, which allows the PSC to preempt certain  local government decisions.

    Birch Valley Solar Project in Tuscola County Faces Local Pushback Over Farmland and State Override, THUMBNET.NET, Jun. 8, 2025,  https://medium.com/michigan-news/birch-valley-solar-project-in-tuscola-county-faces-local-pushback-over-farmland-and-state-override-447da3c4d593; Birch Valley Solar Project, https://birchvalleysolar.com/project-overview/ (last visited July 30, 2025).

  • Confluence Solar Project (Genesee County)

    Opponents of Ranger Power LLC’s plans for a 200-MW, 1,500-acre solar farm collected over 200 signatures for petition against the development and lobbied the township board for changes to the zoning ordinance that may kill it. In December 2022, the Flushing Township Board approved an amendment to the township zoning ordinance that may prevent the project by limiting total area of solar panels to 25% of lot area.   • Mustang Mile Solar Energy (Lenawee County)

    In 2017, Invenergy proposed the 150-MW Mustang Mile Solar project to be located on approximately 2,777 acres in Macon Township. From 2018 to 2020, the township adopted amendments to its solar ordinance to allow large-scale solar facilities as a special land use. However, in 2021, the Planning Commission recommended denial of a permit for the Mustang Mile Solar project on the basis that it did not meet the required standards for a special land use. The Township Board, in a 3-2 vote, approved issuance of a special use permit for the project, despite the Commission’s findings and recommendation to deny it. In 2021, local opponents of the project filed a lawsuit in the Lenawee Circuit Court challenging the Board’s issuance of the permit. The circuit court affirmed the Board’s decision; in its ruling, the court erroneously stated that the Commission had recommended approval of the permit. The opponents appealed the circuit court’s decision to the Michigan Court of Appeals. In October 2025, the court of appeals vacated the circuit court’s decision reasoning that the lower court’s decision was an error unsupported by the record. The matter was remanded to the Board for further proceedings.

Minnesota
State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts (MW) in size and wind projects less than 5 MW in size. Localities may adopt an ordinance to assume jurisdiction over the permitting of wind projects between 5 and 25 MW in size.

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that are 50 MW or larger and wind projects that are 5 MW or larger (unless the local government has an ordinance extending its authority to projects up to 25 MW in size, in which case the state only has authority over the siting of larger projects (i.e., 25 MW or more)). The state also has jurisdiction over energy storage systems with a capacity of 50 MW or more. A site permit from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission (MPUC) is required for projects under state jurisdiction. Under state law, the issuance of a site permit by the MPSC supersedes and preempts all other zoning, building, or land use rules, regulations, or ordinances promulgated by regional, county, local, and special purpose government.

The MPUC must hold at least 1 public hearing before deciding whether to issue a site permit. A final decision must be made by the MPUC within 1 year of receipt of a complete application and within 60 days of receipt of a report from an administrative law judge for solar projects and within 180 days of receipt of a complete application for wind projects.

Minn. Stat. §§ 216E.01, 216E.02, 216E.03, 216E.03 Subd. 3b and 6, 216E.05, 216E.10, 216E.021, 216F.01, 216F.01 Subd. 3, 216.F.02, 216F.04(c), 216F.07, 216F.08, 394.301, 216I.02(6), 216I.02(9), 216I.02(11), 216I.18(1); Minnesota Energy Infrastructure Permitting Act, H.F. 4700, 93rd Leg., 2024 Sess. (Minn. 2024), https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/text.php?number=HF4700&session=ls93&version=list&session_number=0&session_year=2024; Christina Brusven, Minnesota Legislature Passes Historic Permitting Reform Bill, Fredrikson & Byron, P.A., May 22, 2024, https://www.fredlaw.com/alert-minnesota-legislature-passes-historic-permitting-reform-bill; Micah Revell, Minnesota Enacts Sweeping Energy Legislation with Implications for Permitting, Transmission, and Decarbonization, Stinson LLP, May 30, 2024, https://www.stinson.com/newsroom-publications-minnesota-enacts-sweeping-energy-legislation-with-implications-for-permitting-transmission-and-decarbonization.

However, after receiving public comment, the city council rejected the project in October 2020 and implemented a moratorium on solar energy projects while it revised its ordinance to make clear that only small accessory-use systems are allowed.

    After a drawn-out battle between New Era Wind and Goodhue County residents, the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission voted against further authorization of the New Era Wind Farm in August 2013. The MPUC determined that the operation of this wind farm would pose a risk to eagles and other endangered bird species in Goodhue County. New Era Wind announced that it was terminating its plans for the project soon after.

  • Gopher State Solar Project (Renville County)

    In August 2024, Ranger Power submitted an application to construct the 200-MW Gopher State Solar Project on approximately 1,667 acres in the townships of Kingman, Osceola, and Bird Island. Opponents of the project, including county officials, have questioned the estimated costs of decommissioning as insufficient. Local residents also raised concerns of potential visual and noise pollution and impacts to property values. In June 2025, an administrative law judge recommended approval of the permit by the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) subject to special conditions as decided by the PUC. If approved, the developer expects construction to begin in the spring of 2027.

    The McLeod County Board of Commissioners rejected a proposal for a 3.5-acre solar garden on prime farmland. In 2021, the Minnesota Court of Appeals overturned the County Board’s decision. The court found that the Board’s stated concerns about impacts to neighboring property values and prime farmland were arbitrary and capricious and ordered the Board to approve the project.

    In 2025, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Lemon Hill Solar project to be located on approximately 1,945 acres of agricultural land outside Viola and Haverhill townships. In November 2025, at a Minnesota Public Utilities Commission public meeting, a majority of attendees raised concerns about the potential for soil disturbance from the project and its impacts on water supply and property values, and called for increased setbacks. The permitting process remains pending.

    Grant Jones, Residents raise concerns over Lemon Hill Solar Project in public meeting, KTTC, Nov. 19, 2025, https://www.kttc.com/2025/11/20/residents-raise-concerns-over-lemon-hill-solar-project-public-meeting/.

    This 500-acre, 62-MW solar energy complex in southwestern Minnesota faced opposition from local residents who argued that it would lower property values and disrupt their rural lifestyle. Opponents of the project also complained that the developer had not sought out non-prime farmland for the project. The PUC unanimously approved the project in March 2016.

    In 2025, New Leaf Energy proposed the 5-MW Morristown Solar project to be located on approximately 35 acres of agricultural land northeast of Morristown.   • Big Blue Wind Farm (Faribault County)

    This 18-turbine, 36-MW wind farm went online in December 2012. After years of complaints about noise, the PUC intervened in 2017 and discovered that the project’s noise protocol had never been approved. Residents then pushed for the farm to be completely shut down, but the Public Utilities Commission instead ordered the developer to address the problems and issued a warning.

Mississippi

State Siting Framework

The state has principal authority over the siting of all electricity generating projects, including wind and solar energy projects. Projects require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Mississippi Public Service Commission (MPSC). Prior to requesting a CPCN from the MPSC, the project developer must first obtain a franchise from the relevant local government where it intends to provide electric services.

The MPSC must hold a public hearing after receipt of a CPNC application. There is no statutory deadline for the MPSC to reach a final decision on applications.

Miss. Code Ann. §§ 17-1-3, 77-3-11, 77-3-13, 77-3-13(3), 77-3-19.

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Minkar Solar Farm (Lamar County)

    In July 2023, Lamar County residents organized a community meeting to express opposition to the proposed 90-MW, 1,700-acre Minkar solar farm. Residents raised concerns about property values impacts, destruction of agricultural land, displacement of wildlife, and more. Two residents created signs, an online petition, and a social media group in opposition to the project; as of February 2024, the petition had 336 signatures. At the time, developer Lighthouse BP was conducting studies of the proposed site and was planning on holding a public meeting. The Lamar County Board of Supervisors will ultimately decide on whether to approve the project.

    Michael Clark, Lamar County residents plan town hall to push back against proposed solar farm, WDAM, July 26, 2023, https://www.wdam.com/2023/07/26/lamar-county-residents-plan-town-hall-push-back-against-proposed-solar-farm/; Hasket Burns, Residents Voice Opposition to Proposed Solar Farm in Lamar County, The Pine Belt News, Aug. 1, 2023, https://www.hubcityspokes.com/local-content/residents-voice-opposition-proposed-solar-farm-lamar-county; Say NO to Solar Farms in Lamar County, Change.org, https://www.change.org/p/say-no-to-solar-farms-in-lamar-county (last visited Feb. 1, 2024).

  • Soul City Solar (Hinds County)

    In 2021, Apex Clean Energy began acquiring leases for a proposed 6,000-acre, 396-MW solar farm and 70-MW battery storage facility. Nearby residents organized in opposition to the project, sending a letter to the Hinds County Planning and Zoning Department, along with a Change.org petition with over 1,000 signatures. The Hinds County Planning Commission voted against recommending the project; however, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors approved the project in a 3-2 vote on June 17, 2024. On April 10, 2025, the Circuit Court affirmed the decision of the Hinds County Board of Supervisors. On May 9, 2025, a local opponent appealed the Circuit’s Court decision to the Mississippi Supreme Court. On August 12, 2025, a public hearing on the project was held by the Mississippi Public Service Commission (PSC), which must issue a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity for the project before construction can begin. The Commissioners heard testimony from the developer, as well as supporters and opponents of the project. The PSC did not rule on the certificate given that the appeal of the project approval remains pending in the Supreme Court.

Missouri

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over electric generating projects under the Missouri Zoning and Planning Enabling Act (though renewable energy facilities are not explicitly mentioned).

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for the local government to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

 

 

Mo. Rev. Stat. § 89.010 et seq.

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Pending
  • Gateway Trails Solar Project (Clay County)

    Solis Renewables has proposed a 20-MW solar facility called Gateway Trails Solar Project, to be developed on approximately 112 acres of privately-owned land in Clay County. The project has faced local opposition, with some advocating for housing development over the deployment of renewable energy. A Facebook group called “Missouri Coalition for the Environment” circulated a petition in support of the project. On April 1, 2025, the Planning and Zoning Commission held a public meeting at which opponents of the project raised concerns about the region’s housing shortage, potential impacts to wildlife habitat, decommissioning costs and fire safety. In response to the concerns, the developer is scheduled to submit a revised conditional permit application at the next planning commission meeting in July 2025. The modified proposal would include vegetative screening buffers with no barbed wire, emergency access plans and safety training, and a fully funded decommissioning bond.

    Elizabeth Barnt, Proposed Excelsior Springs Solar Farm Faces Pushback at County Zoning Hearing, Excelsior Citizen, Jun. 22, 2025, https://excelsiorcitizen.com/proposed-excelsior-springs-solar-farm-faces-pushback-at-county-zoning-hearing/; Missouri Coalition for the Environment, Facebook, https://www.facebook.com/100064694197966/posts/1079882744178189 (last visited August 4, 2025), Gateway Trail Solar Project, https://gatewaytrailssolar.com/ (last visited August 4, 2025).

  • Grain Belt Express Tiger Connector Expansion (Callaway and Chariton Counties)

    A Facebook group with 600 followers called “Callaway County Missouri Solar Invasion” organized residents to oppose a 40-mile connector to the 800-mile Grain Belt Express (GBX) transmission line. Opponents of the project raised concerns about visual impacts and loss of farmland caused by the solar projects that the transmission line will support. In October 2022, a coalition of agricultural groups in Missouri issued a joint statement opposing an amendment to GBX’s plan that would include a new transmission line and expanded power capacity. Missouri regulators granted the project final approval in October 2023. In October 2024, the state’s court of appeals ruled that the Chariton County government could not block the construction of the project by refusing permission to cross its county roads. On July 23, 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy announced the cancellation of a $4.9 billion conditional federal loan guarantee for phase one of the project from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri.

    John Hanna, Trump administration canceled a $4.9B loan guarantee for a line to deliver green power, AP NEWS, Jul. 23, 2025, https://apnews.com/article/green-energy-transmission-line-grain-belt-express-6d674ba10fc2d5700133989695e838ec; Matthew Zeitlin, After Trump Phone Call, DOE Cancels $5 Billion for Grain Belt Express, HEATMAP, Jul. 23, 2025, https://heatmap.news/sparks/doe-grain-belt-express-guarantee; Rudi Keller, Grain Belt Express clears another legal hurdle with Missouri appeals court ruling, Missouri Independent, Oct. 15, 2024, https://missouriindependent.com/briefs/grain-belt-express-clears-another-legal-hurdle-with-missouri-appeals-court-ruling/; Grain Belt v. Montana

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over electric generating projects under the Montana county and municipal zoning statute (though renewable energy facilities are not explicitly mentioned).

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for the local government to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

Mont. Code Ann. §§ 76-2-201 et seq., 76-2-301 et seq.

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

    Pattern Energy proposed a 22-turbine project in Sweet Grass County. Four companies that own neighboring land initiated a legal action alleging nuisance. Nebraska

State Siting Framework

Local governments may adopt ordinances to encourage wind and solar energy development. However, the state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities. All projects must be approved by the Nebraska Power Review Board. The Board must hold a public hearing within 60 days of receiving an application for project approval and must make a final decision on the application within 60 days thereafter. The Board may waive the hearing requirement in certain instances if it finds it unnecessary.

Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 66-913, 70-1001.01(4), 70-1012, 70-1013, 70-1014.02(2)

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

    Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
    In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code to require that wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings. The county also set the following setback requirements: 2 times turbine height from non-participating property lines, 3.5 times turbine height from non-participating dwellings, and 2 times turbine height from participating dwellings. The county defined turbine height as hub height plus rotor radius. In 2019, Lancaster County once again updated its wind energy regulations to require a 1-mile setback from non-participating dwellings.

    In April 2024, the Otoe County Board of Commissioners enacted a moratorium on conditional use permits for commercial solar projects, which was extended in May 2024 and August 2024. Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Bluestem Energy Solutions’ Knox County Solar Project (Knox County)

    On September 18, 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted to deny a conditional use permit to Bluestone Energy Solutions to construct a 325-acre solar project.

    Proceedings of the Knox County Board of Supervisors, Sept. 18, 2024, at 5-6, https://knoxcountyne.gov/posting_files/pdfs/board/minutes/2024/20240918_093516_board_minutes.pdf.

  • Cass County Solar (Cass County)

    In 2021, NextEra Energy proposed to develop the 1.5-MW Cass County solar project on approximately 2,000 acres of farmland west of Murray. In February 2025, the Cass County Board denied a conditional use permit for the project, citing local opposition to it based on concerns about its impact on property values. The Board also noted that the priority of the county’s development plan is to preserve agriculture.

    Dan Swanson, County rejects Cass County Solar, NEWS CHANNEL NEBRASKA, Feb. 14, 2025, https://rivercountry.newschannelnebraska.com/story/52367495/county-rejects-cass-county-solar%20LINKS.

Projects with Status Pending
  • Greeley Wind Project (Greeley County)

    NextEra Energy Resources is developing the 41-turbine, 115-MW Greeley Wind project. NextEra has planned for the project to begin operations by December 2026, subject to local and state approvals. The Greeley County Board of Commissioners approved a special use permit for NextEra despite the vocal opposition. Opponents voiced health concerns related to noise, vibrations, and shadow flicker generated by the turbines; environmental concerns related to the concrete bases and decommissioning of blades; and economic concerns related to property values and farm income. Local residents voiced opposition on the Facebook group Greeley County Alliance for Wise Energy.

    Nancy Gaarder, Public safety, economic opportunity, China: Renewable energy debate runs hot in Nebraska, Flatwater Free Press, Feb. 16, 2024, https://flatwaterfreepress.org/public-safety-economic-opportunity-china-renewable-energy-debate-runs-hot-in-nebraska/; AP, Wind Farm developers face headwinds from opposition, misinformation, Daily Reporter, July 29, 2024, https://dailyreporter.com/2024/07/29/wind-farm-developers-face-headwinds-from-opposition-misinformation/.

  • K-Junction Solar (York County)

    OPPD energy has proposed a 310-MW solar project in York County called K-Junction Solar. In October 2023, over 100 residents attended a meeting at which many residents expressed concern about the project’s environmental and economic impacts, including impacts on the local agriculture industry, while other residents supported the potential for agrivoltaics and potential positive impacts on the local economy.   • Kilgore Wind Farm (Cherry County)

    In July 2016, the Cherry County Planning Commission formally recommended against granting a conditional land use permit to Bluestem Sandhills to construct the Kilgore Wind Project, which was then planned to be a 30-turbine wind farm in Cherry County. The decision was made at a meeting attended by over 200 individuals that lasted until 2:00 a.m. A local opposition group raised arguments about potential impacts on birds and wetlands. In October 2019, the Cherry County Board granted a conditional use permit to a 19-turbine plan for the project. A group called Preserve the Sandhills LLC, which claimed to have 500 members, filed an appeal challenging the decision in Cherry County District Court the following month. In August 2020, District Judge Kosizek denied a motion to dismiss, allowing the suit to proceed. In June 2020, the Cherry County Board granted a 4-year extension for the completion of the wind turbine project while the suit was pending, which the project opponents claimed was improper. However, the Cherry County District Court held that it did not have jurisdiction to consider objections to the extension, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court of Nebraska in 2021. On February 24, 2023, the Nebraska Supreme Court dismissed appeals from Preserve the Sandhills LLC, paving the way for the project to move forward.

Nevada

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar and wind projects that are less than 70 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of solar and wind projects that are 70 MW or larger in size. Such larger projects must be permitted by the Nevada Public Utilities Commission (NPUC).

The NPUC must make a decision within 150 days of receiving a permit application or, if a federal agency is required to conduct an environmental analysis of the facility, within 120 days. There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the permit review process.

State law prohibits local governments from adopting unreasonable restrictions on wind and solar development on private land and mandates that local zoning regulations must be designed “to promote systems which use solar or wind energy.”

Nev. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 278.02077, 278.0208, 278.250(n), 704.860, 704.865, 704.8905.

State-Level Restrictions

No restrictive state laws, regulations, or policies were found at this time.

    In 2023, a number of developers including NextEra Energy, Invenergy, ConnectGen, and Arevia, proposed the Esmeralda Seven Solar Project on approximately 62,300 acres of public lands across the western Nevada desert. The project would combine 7 separate developments, including solar energy panels and battery storage facilities, for an aggregated total capacity of 6,200 MW. Several local community members expressed strong opposition to the project and expressed concern about its size and the impact on the largely undeveloped desert land. In April 2025, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM) released the final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for the project, and the record of decision on permitting was expected by July 2025. The decision was not issued in June, however. In October 2025, BLM’s online register listed the project as “cancelled” with no further explanation.

New Hampshire

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal authority over the siting of wind and solar projects that are less than 30 megawatts (MW) in size. However, the state may choose to exercise discretionary jurisdiction over certain projects with a capacity of 5 MW to 30 MW, either on its own motion or by petition. State law prohibits local governments from adopting “unreasonable” limits on small-scale wind projects (0.1 MW or less) including, for instance, bans on construction or excessive setbacks (defined as setbacks that are more than 150% of the system height).

The state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities that are 30 megawatts (MW) or larger, as well as projects over which it has exercised discretionary jurisdiction. A certificate from the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee (NHSEC) is required for all such projects. The NHSEC must decide whether to accept a certificate application within 60 days. If accepted, all state agencies having permitting or regulatory authority over the project must submit to the NHSEC draft permit conditions within 150 days, and a final decision on the relevant parts of the application within 240 days. The NHSEC is required to make a final decision on whether to issue a certificate for the project within 1 year of receipt of the application.

The applicant must hold at least 1 public information hearing 30 days before submitting a certificate application to the NHSEC. In addition, the applicant must hold at least 1 public information hearing within 30 days of the NHSEC accepting the application. The NHSEC must hold at least 1 public hearing in each county involved within 90 days of accepting the application.

N.H. RSA §§ 162-H:2:VII, 162-H:2:XII[IN1] , 162-H:7:VI; 162-H:10, 674:17(I)(j), 674:62, 674:63

New Jersey

State Siting Framework

Local governments regulate the permitting of small-scale renewable energy projects with a capacity of 0.1 MW or less. State law prohibits “unreasonable” local restrictions on small wind energy systems (i.e., those consisting of a single turbine and used for onsite consumption), including bans on construction, excessive setbacks (defined as setbacks greater than 150% of the system height), limits on tower height, and caps on noise of less than 55 decibels. Additionally, developers of offshore wind projects have the right to appeal to the state when a local government blocks approvals needed for the project (e.g., for cable landings).

The state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities that are larger than 0.1MW. Such projects require a permit from the Office of Permitting and Project Navigation, within the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJ DEP). Projects may also require additional permits from other state agencies depending on the location and nature of the project.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process at either the state or local level and no deadline for the NJ DEP or local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

N.J. Stat. §§ 40:55D-66.11, 40:55D-66.12, 40:55D-66.16; J.A.C. § 7:50-5.36; Wayne Parry, N.J. uses new law to bypass local approvals for offshore wind project, Associated Press, Feb. 17, 2023, https://whyy.org/articles/new-jersey-offshore-wind-projectnew-law-bypass-local-approval/.

New Mexico

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over energy generation projects, including wind and solar energy projects, that are less than 300 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal siting authority over larger facilities (i.e., 300 MW or more). Approval by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission is required for those larger projects. If the Commission finds that an existing state, county, or municipal land use regulation is “unreasonably burdensome” as to a proposed project and that “compliance with the regulation is not in the interest of the public convenience and necessity,” that regulation “shall be inapplicable and void as to the siting.”

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission must decide an application within 6 months of filing. A public hearing is typically required prior to the Commission’s decision, but the Commission may approve an application without a hearing if no protest is filed within 60 days of the application.

N.M. Stat. Ann. §§ 3-18-32, 3-21-1, 62-9-3(B), 62-9-3(C), 62-9-3(G), 62-9-3(K), see also Steven Ferrey, Siting Technology, Land-Use Energized, 66 Cath. U. L. Rev. 1, 25-26 (2017), https://scholarship.law.edu/lawreview/vol66/iss1/6/.

    Lisa Dunlap, Community solar project denied permit, Roswell Daily Record, Oct. 20, 2021, https://www.rdrnews.com/news/local/community-solar-project-denied-permit/article_e3165de8-5ff9-5380-86cb-dda7ae5ac0b2.html; Lisa Dunlap, Company, landowners plan solar project appeal, Roswell Daily Record, Nov. 30, 2021, https://www.rdrnews.com/news/local/company-landowners-plan-solar-project-appeal/article_529170f8-4784-5ee8-9fa1-6bda5f4f7011.html

  • Rancho Viejo Solar Project (Santa Fe County)

    The Rancho Viejo Solar Project, a 680-acre, 96-MW solar farm with a 2-acre, 48-MW battery storage facility proposed by AES, has faced resistance from the local community. Residents have established the Clean Energy Coalition for Santa Fe County and New Mexicans for Responsible Renewable Energy to fight against the project. The latter started an online petition directed at Santa Fe County, asking that officials either deny the project’s conditional use permit application or issue a moratorium and amend county codes before considering the project further. Residents have expressed distrust toward the company and argued that the county has failed to adequately engage the community. A resident submitted in August 2023 a Notice of Violation to Santa Fe County and filed in September 2023 a complaint with the New Mexico Attorney General, alleging that the County’s meetings with AES violated New Mexico’s Open Meetings Act. The County denied the allegations, and the Attorney General responded that no violations occurred. In August 2024, residents attended a county meeting at which AES presented a revised plan that sought to address the community’s concerns. Opponents have stated that the project should not be located near residential areas, due to the risk of fires and environmental contamination. Supporters have stated that the technology has become much safer and emphasized the importance of addressing climate change.

    Nicholas Gilmore, Residents still oppose Rancho Viejo Solar Project despite changes, Santa Fe New Mexican, Aug 22, 2024, https://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/local_news/aes-presents-new-plans-for-solar-farm-raising-ire-of-county-residents/article_128feeea-60ab-11ef-ae7d-7bc4a9069afb.html; Michael Benanav, Burning question: What’s the right place for a solar farm?, Searchlight New Mexico, Mar 13, 2024, https://searchlightnm.org/burning-question-whats-the-right-place-for-a-solar-farm/; Sign the Petition, New Mexicans for Responsible Renewable Energy, https://www.nmresponsible.com/copy-of-get-involved-1 (last visited Feb. 2, 2024); Nicholas Gilmore, Rancho Viejo Solar faces obstacles to breaking ground off N.M. 14, Santa Fe New Mexican, May 20, 2023, https://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/local_news/rancho-viejo-solar-faces-obstacles-to-breaking-ground-off-n-m-14/article_cac12438-ee7f-11ed-b6e5-5731b7fc4f54.html; Nicholas Gilmore, Eldorado resident; Notice not given for change to county code for solar project, Santa Fe New Mexican, Aug. 20, 2023, https://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/local_news/eldorado-resident-notice-not-given-for-change-to-county-code-for-solar-project/article_61fe3b2e-3d18-11ee-84a7-ffed0059fac2.html.

New York

State Siting Framework

Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy facilities, including wind and solar energy projects, that are less than 25 megawatts (MW) in size.

The state has principal siting authority over larger renewable energy facilities (25 MW or larger). Approval by the state Office of Renewable Energy Siting (ORES) is required for those larger projects. Additionally, project developers may elect to have smaller projects, with a capacity of 20 to 25 MW, approved by ORES rather than the relevant local government. ORES also has jurisdiction over projects previously under the jurisdiction of the state siting board pursuant to Article 10 of the New York Public Service Law and over co-located energy storage systems and associated electric transmission systems less than 10 miles in length.

Project developers are required to consult with local governments about local laws prior to applying for project approval from ORES. However, ORES “may elect not to apply, in whole or in part, any local law or ordinance which would otherwise be applicable if it makes a finding that, as applied to the proposed major renewable energy facility, it is unreasonably burdensome in view of the [state’s climate] targets and the environmental benefits of the proposed major renewable energy facility.”

ORES must decide whether an application is complete within 60 days of its filing. ORES must issue draft permit conditions within 60 days, and issue a final permit decision within 1 year, after determining that the application is complete. The applicant must hold a public meeting with the local government and with community members at least 60 days before filing a permit application.

N.Y. Public Service Law, Art. 8 §§136-148; N.Y. Town Law §261 et seq.; N.Y. Village Law §7-700, 19 N.Y.C.R.R. §§ 900-1.1 to 900- 15.2, 900-5.1, 900-1.3; see also Michael B. Gerrard & Edward McTiernan, New York’s New Statute on Siting Renewable Energy Facilities, New York Law Journal, Vol. 263, No. 93, May 14, 2020, https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/3026/.

State-Level Restrictions

Restrictions with Status In effect
  • New York Public Authority Law. § 1005(27-a)(b)

    Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (wind) | Rule 1: Ban/Moratorium (solar)
    On May 3, 2023, the state adopted a law directing the New York Power Authority (NYPA) to develop renewable energy projects “to support the state’s renewable energy goals established pursuant to the climate leadership and community protection act.” While the law generally encourages renewable energy development, it places two significant limitations on where renewable energy facilities may be sited. First, the law specifies that NYPA shall not develop renewable energy generation projects on “land used in agricultural production . . . unless [the] project is in furtherance of an agrivoltaics project” (i.e., unless the project is designed to accommodate dual-use farming and energy production). Second, the law provides that NYPA “shall . . . not build on lands located upon any Native American territory or reservation . . . except through voluntary sale or other agreement for such use with the consent of the relevant nation.”

    2023 N.Y. Laws, ch. 56, part QQ, sec. 1 (to be codified N.Y. Pub. Auth. Law. § 1005(27-a)(b)).

Contested Projects

Projects with Status Canceled
  • Black Oak Wind Farm (Tompkins County)

    The Black Oak Wind Farm, a proposed 7-turbine, 16-MW project, was first conceived in 2006. However, in December 2017, the developer canceled the project. The developer blamed the Town of Enfield’s moratorium and other actions, which effectively held up the project for two years and drove the company into bankruptcy.

    Brian Crandall, Black Oak Wind Farm cancelled, Ithaca Voice, Dec. 31, 2017, https://ithacavoice.org/2017/12/black-oak-wind-farm-cancelled/.

  • Bulls Head Battery Storage Project (Richmond County)

    In January 2023, New Leaf withdrew its application to build a 20 MWh battery storage facility in Staten Island amid community opposition. Opponents expressed concerns about fire risk and argued that the facility was too close to a church and six local schools.

    Jessica Jones-Gorman, Plans withdrawn for community-opposed lithium-ion battery storage system on Staten Island, silive.com, Jan. 13, 2023, https://www.silive.com/business/2023/01/plans-withdrawn-for-community-opposed-lithium-ion-battery-storage-system-on-staten-island.html.

  • Cape Vincent Wind Project (Jefferson County)

    In 2014, after a 10-year battle to develop a 200- to 285-MW wind project in the Town of Cape Vincent, BP Wind Energy formally withdrew its application. Seasonal residents opposed the project due to concerns about impacts to property values, while many year-round residents supported the project because of the revenues it would bring.

    BP ‘terminates’ controversial plans for Cape Vincent wind farm, WWNYTV, Feb. 26, 2014, https://www.wind-watch.org/news/2014/02/27/bp-terminates-controversial-plans-for-cape-vincent-wind-farm/

  • Chapman Road Community Solar (Oneida County)

    In February 2025, U.S. Light Energy proposed the 5-MW solar project called Chapman Road Community Solar to be developed on approximately 23 acres of a 70-acre parcel in the town of New Hartford. On February 12, 2025, the New Hartford Town Board unanimously rejected the proposal following a public meeting in which local residents voted 125 – 2 against the project, primarily because it was proposed in a residential area.

    Alexis Manore, New Hartford Town Board strikes down Chapman Road community solar proposal, DAILY SENTINEL, Feb. 13, 2025, https://www.romesentinel.com/news/new-hartford-town-board-chapman-road-solar-project/article_a87fcc8c-ea16-11ef-a9f5-2314a3db79e4.html; Thomas Tallarino, New Hartford Board Denies Potential Chapman Road Solar Project Due to Negative Feedback, NEWS CHANNEL 2, Feb. 13, 2025, https://www.wktv.com/news/new-hartford-board-denies-potential-chapman-road-solar-project-due-to-negative-feedback/article_0a33b31e-e9b6-11ef-bbc0-67e36a343ffe.html.

  • EverPower Wind Farm (Cattaraugus County)

    In 2014, the Allegany Town Board rejected a proposed 29 turbine wind farm in Cattaraugus County. Local opponents had contested the project for eight years leading up to the decision.

    Rick Miller, Proposed town of Allegany wind farm shelved by Terra-Gen, Olean Times Herald, Nov. 17, 2023, https://www.oleantimesherald.com/news/proposed-town-of-allegany-wind-farm-shelved-by-terra-gen/article_dcb7b8c8-858d-11ee-b393-8348bc62f63d.html.

  • Florida Wind 1, LLC Wind Turbine Project (Montgomery County)

    In 2021, New Leaf Energy LLC submitted a proposal to build a single 4.5-MW wind turbine, standing 650 feet tall, on a 135-acre vacant property in the Town of Florida, New York. In October 2024, after several years of review, the Florida Planning Board unanimously denied approval. Local opponents had raised concerns about visual impacts, community character, shadow flicker, and noise.

    Ashley Onyon, Florida Planning Board Rejects Proposed Wind Turbine, Concluding Multi-Year Review, THE RECORDER, Oct. 9, 2024, https://www.dailygazette.com/the_recorder/news/town-florida-wind-turbine/article_43f0e0f4-85a7-11ef-8152-8f5d964960e1.html.

  • Galloo Island Wind Project (Jefferson County)

    In February 2019, Apex abandoned plans to construct a 108-MW wind farm on Galloo Island. The project faced opposition from residents concerned about impacts to property values and a retired wildlife biologist, who raised concerns about the presence of a bald eagle nest near the project site.

    Marcus Wolf, Opponents applaud withdrawal, backers lament, Watertown Daily Times, Feb. 12, 2019, https://www.nny360.com/news/opponents-applaud-withdrawal-backers-lament/article_aa746d96-8999-533b-b186-09c947635231.html.

  • Gate of Heaven Solar Farm (Westchester County)

    On September 2, 2021, the Mount Pleasant Planning Board voted to deny an application to build a 5.75-MW solar farm in the Gate of Heaven cemetery. Saw Mill River Audubon and the Westchester County Planning Board wrote letters in opposition to the project. In denying the project, Mount Pleasant Planning Board members focused on the number of trees that would need to be cleared and the potential impacts that such tree-clearing could have on mudslides.

    Michael Gold, Mount Pleasant Planning Board Rejects Gate of Heaven Solar Farm, Examiner News, Sept. 6, 2021, https://www.theexaminernews.com/mount-pleasant-planning-board-rejects-gate-of-heaven-solar-farm.

  • Kirkville Solar (Onondaga County)

    In 2025, New Leaf Energy proposed the 5-MW Kirkville Solar project to be located on approximately 25 acres of land in the Town of Sullivan. A public hearing on the project was scheduled for November 13, 2025, but had to be postponed after close to a hundred local residents (more than could fit in the venue) attended. Although no actual hearing was held at that time, opponents of the proposed facility informally voiced concerns about the project’s impact on flooding, obstruction of views in the area, and public safety. In December 2025, the developer withdrew its application for an area variance permit, citing uncertainty as to whether it would be obtained in time to have the facility operational by December 2027.

    Kirkville Solar/New Leaf Energy, Withdrawal of Area Variance Letter, December 8, 2025, https://www.townofsullivanny.gov/sites/g/files/vyhlif3886/f/news/nle_area_variance_withdrawal_letter.pdf; Allie Elkins, New solar farm proposal in Kirkville drums up controversy, WSYR, Nov. 12, 2025, https://www.localsyr.com/news/local-news/new-solar-farm-proposal-in-kirkville-drums-up-controversy/; Allie Elkins, Kirkville solar farm public hearing delayed because of high turnout, WSYR, Nov. 13, 2025, https://www.localsyr.com/news/local-news/kirkville-solar-farm-public-hearing-delayed-because-of-high-turnout/.

  • Lighthouse Wind Project (Niagara and Orleans Counties)

    In January 2018, the Somerset Town Board passed restrictions that would effectively prevent approval and construction of the proposed 201-MW, 70-turbine Lighthouse Wind project, unless the state were to override those restrictions under Article 10 of the New York Public Service Law. In September 2022, after eight years of contentious public hearings and lawsuits, the developer formally abandoned the project.

  • Mad River Wind Farm (Jefferson and Oswego Counties)

    The proposed 88-turbine, 350-MW Mad River Wind Farm in the Tug Hill region of upstate New York encountered opposition from the Tug Hill Tomorrow Land Trust due to potential ecological impacts. In June 2019, supporters of the project accused the Worth town board of secretly passing a law that severely restricted wind farm construction in April and then claiming the next month that they would table a vote on the law. In December 2020, the developer abandoned the project.
